speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BANK OF CANADA
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday morning Mr. James Coyne, governor of the Bank of Canada, issued a statement, which has been widely circulated, concerning his tenure of office as governor. It would not be appropriate at this point in the proceedings of the house to comment in detail on his published statement sentence by sentence or on its defiant and provocative character. At this stage I must confine myself to placing before the house the essential facts, virtually none of which appear in that statement.
During Mr. Coyne's period in office there has been a steady and deplorable deterioration in the relations of the Bank of Canada with the public. The governor, by a course of ill considered action and a series of public declarations of policy on public issues quite outside the realm of central banking, and by his rigid and doctrinaire expression of views, often and openly incompatible with government policy, has embroiled the bank in continuous controversy with strong political overtones.
Mr. Coyne's rigid attitude on the maintenance of high interest rates is one example. The government's policy is expansionist, aimed at the creation of more trade, more production and more jobs. The policies advocated by Mr. Coyne are restrictionist, restrictive of trade, restrictive of production and restrictive of jobs. The government has exercised patience in the hope of avoiding
[Mr. Herridge.l

further controversy pending the expiry of his term of office on December 31 next, but its hopes have been frustrated by Mr. Coyne and it can no longer postpone decisive action.
Matters of high importance are awaiting decision and co-operative action by both the bank and the government. The need of teamwork between them and leadership by them has never been greater. It has become impossible to expect this kind of co-operation as long as the present governor remains in office. It was perfectly plain to the government that whatever assurances Mr. Coyne might give of co-operation for the future, the public could have no confidence that Bank of Canada policy would support government policy, having in mind the frequent public declarations by the governor which clearly run counter to the policies of the government.
Mr. Coyne has, as I shall explain shortly, lost the confidence of the board of directors of the Bank of Canada. He does not possess the confidence of the government.
On May 30, on the instructions of the government, I asked Mr. Coyne to tender his resignation to the board of directors of the bank. I further asked that he do so before the regular board meeting to be held in Quebec on June 12 and 13, so that action on the resignation might be taken by the board1 at its meeting. I gave him an ample statement of the reasons for the course the government was following. The main reason was that the government was convinced that Mr. Coyne's continuation in office as governor of the Bank of Canada would stand in the way of the implementation of a comprehensive, sound and responsible economic program designed to raise the levels of employment and production in Canada. After an hour's discussion he asked to be allowed to think the matter over. Presumably his published statement yesterday is his reply to the government's request.
Section 6 of the Bank of Canada Act provides as follows:
The governor and deputy governor shall be appointed by the directors with the approval of the governor in council.
As is well known, Mr. Coyne was appointed by the board of directors with approval of the then governor in council in December, 1954, for a seven year term as governor expiring December 31, 1961. This term has six and a half months to run. Had Mr. Coyne complied with the government's request, the board of directors of the bank would have been in a position at its meeting in the last two days to take action on the resignation and, if so disposed, to appoint a successor with the approval of the governor in council.
I had hoped to announce in the house today that this course had been followed and that

the whole matter would have been handled with dignity and consideration. Mr. Coyne, however, has chosen to reject the request and to provoke a controversy.
Mr. Coyne has not contented himself with disregarding a request from the government. The board of directors met at Quebec on Monday and Tuesday. The subject of Mr. Coyne's tenure was discussed both days. Mr. Coyne himself introduced the subject at the board's meeting on Monday morning. Both at the morning session and again at the afternoon session that day he delivered a lengthy defence of his administration. Discussion followed. I am informed that Mr. Coyne was made fully aware on Monday that the board would ask for his resignation if he did not choose to submit it.
The board meeting resumed on Tuesday morning at 9.30; that was yesterday. When it became clear that the board was about to introduce a resolution requesting the immediate resignation of Mr. Coyne, he asked to be excused and asked the board to consider other matters of business while he was out. He returned to the meeting at 12.15 o'clock to inform the board that he had issued a statement to the press at 11 o'clock. This statement was apparently released simultaneously in Quebec and Ottawa. I am also informed that he read the press statement to the board and intimated that he would not resign even if the board of directors requested him to do so.
With Mr. Coyne in the chair the board then proceeded to vote on the following resolution:
That it is in the best interests of the Bank of Canada that the governor do immediately tender his resignation to the board of directors of the bank and further that this action and decision on the part of the board has been taken after prolonged consideration and with regret.
Mr. Coyne polled the directors. The resolution was carried by a vote of nine to one. Mr. Coyne did not vote. Having declared the motion carried, Mr. Coyne then immediately adjourned the meeting.
In doing so he not only defied the formally expressed wish of the board that he should resign immediately in the interests of the bank; he made it impossible for them to proceed to consider what action might be taken in the face of this defiance. It is of particular significance that Mr. Coyne deliberately issued his own press release prepared in advance of the board meeting before the board had reached its decision, and in the knowledge that the board was about to reach a decision. In doing so he left the public with the false impression that the only request for his resignation had come from the government.

As I indicated earlier, it is not my intention to comment in detail on Mr. Coyne's statement. I should like, however, to make two observations. First, by referring to a-I quote his words-"mysterious and alarming'' program which the government is contemplating, Mr. Coyne may have left a certain false impression with the public. Perhaps the best way to dispel this impression is for me to say at once that Mr. Coyne has not been told of the contents of the forthcoming budget and, therefore, has no right whatsoever to express views about it. Second, Mr. Coyne has asserted that he has been given no indication of disagreement with his views on economic policy. In my last two budgets and in various other public statements it has been clear for some time that there have been major differences of opinion with the frequently expressed views of the governor on economic matters.
The earnest efforts of the board of directors and the government to handle this unpleasant matter with dignity and with consideration for Mr. Coyne have thus been frustrated by him. The house will be able to judge whether this was the action of a governor with a proper sense of responsibility to the board of directors of the very important public institution of which he has been governor for the past six and a half years.
I have already indicated that under the terms of the Bank of Canada Act, in appointing the governor the board of directors is the appointing body and the governor in council is the approving body. The board has now asked for his resignation and the government has asked for his resignation. He on his part has asserted his determination to remain in office, though unwanted, for the remaining six and a half months of his seven year term.
Mr. Coyne has referred to his pension claims. Prior to February 15, 1960 Mr. Coyne under present circumstances of age and service would have become entitled on retirement this year to a life pension of slightly less than $12,000 per annum. As the result of a by-law passed by the board that day he claims to have acquired immediate entitlement to a life pension of $25,000 per annum on retirement this year at the age of approximately 50 years.

Here is what the minister said on February 21, as reported at page 2258 of Hansard:
I say that the responsibility owed by the Bank of Canada is to parliament... It is a direct responsibility.
Then the minister went on to refer to the management of the bank on page 2260 of Hansard. He said:
The government has no power whatsoever, once appointments are made, to change them; only parliament can do that.
Then the minister, in defiance of those statements, on May 30 calls in the governor of the bank and demands his resignation. What did the minister say on February 21, the same day, a little later? Let me read from page 2265 of Hansard:
Let us take the extreme case of a headlong clash, Mr. Speaker.

Now the minister, after three months, tells us that there has been a headlong clash going on for months and years between the government and the bank, in spite of the efforts we on this side of the house have made to get the minister to tell us what he thinks of the policy of the governor of the bank and his statement that there has been a headlong clash. The minister took this position when he was speaking in the House of Commons on February 21. He said:
Let us take the extreme case of a headlong clash, Mr. Speaker. In a situation of that nature-
This is the Minister of Finance speaking, who spoke this morning in a very different vein:
In a situation of that nature the government would have no power whatever to terminate the terms of office of the directors or the governor. In that situation all it could do would be to go to parliament, as the Leader of the Opposition said yesterday in effect. That is all it could do. The government has not been given by parliament any power or authority over the bank or its senior officials or directors in that situation.
The Prime Minister had something to say about this, too. He said in a broadcast to the nation on October 1, 1959:
I point out that the Bank of Canada, not the government, controls the money supply in Canada.
Incidentally, that has been denied recently by the governor of the bank himself, and it has been denied by us from this side of the house many times. The Prime Minister continued:
The bank was set up under law by act of parliament. It is independent and autonomous. It has one master, parliament, and through parliament, the people. That is the law. It has been the law for almost 25 years. But, as with any law passed by parliament the Bank of Canada Act is, of course-as the Bank Act is-subject to review and amendment.
Surely the most important issue must have arisen between the governor of the bank and the government. The minister said this morning that this issue had been developing over the months and, indeed, for a long time, though he never indicated in this house during any of the debates we have had on this subject that any such issue was developing at all. If that issue was developing; if the Minister of Finance had had these feelings toward the governor of the bank which he expressed this morning in such strong terms, why has he not risen in the House of Commons in the past and told us about them?

Was there ever a clearer case for a committee of parliament being set up to inquire into a matter of such importance, when the governor and the minister are in complete contradiction even as to the facts?
The other point the minister made dealt with pensions. According to the governor in his statement, this was brought up as one reason why, perhaps, the governor should resign; because the directors of the bank in February, 1960 unanimously took certain action with regard to pensions. Now, on May 30, 1961 the minister gets very indignant about that, and has the effrontery to tell us in this house that he did not know about it. I ask the minister now if the deputy minister has ever reported previously about that meeting. If the minister cannot find out from his own deputy


what goes on at meetings of this kind he is hardly fit to be Minister of Finance.
The minister has been very active trying to find out from the board of directors, since, what went on at that meeting and at other meetings. This was action taken by the board of directors in accordance with their powers. Does the minister object to that action? If so he should fire all the other directors, too. He cannot fire Mr. Bryden because Mr. Bryden has resigned. And let us not forget that two thirds of the board of directors who took this decision were appointed by the present government.
The Minister of Finance who tells this house that neither he nor his government have any responsibility for monetary policy, now says he really must have some responsibility with regard to bank pensions. That is a strange attitude for the minister to take; and if he is trying to force the governor of the Bank of Canada out of office because of some pension difficulty I claim, to use the minister's own words, that it is very undignified-and I could use language much worse than that to discuss tactics of that kind.
That is the situation, Mr. Speaker, and I shall conclude by saying this; that nothing the minister has said this morning is in any way satisfactory as an explanation of the shocking and irresponsible action of the government in this matter. It is not a question of the policy of the board or of the governor of the Bank of Canada; it is a question of the relationship between the government and the Bank of Canada, and that relationship has been shown up in the last few days in a fashion which will cause lack of confidence in the financial community of this country and which may well be a shocking example of government interference with or injustice toward a man who has been a devoted public servant, whatever one might think of his policy or his words.

Mr. Speaker, without doubt the house has listened with great interest to the somewhat lengthy elucidation of a long standing enigma, but what the minister had to say in previous statements in no way indicated to the house that the situation he has now described actually existed. I think that is proven by the record, and there is no reason to quote it again. The members of this group are of the opinion that the minister has not been frank with the house or the country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the minister said his main reason-we noticed he emphasized the word "main", because apparently there are subsidiary reasons which have also been given-for the government's action is that the governor is standing in the way

of certain policies to which the government intends to give effect, to improve the economy of this country. That is in direct contradiction to the correspondence that has been circulated quite recently by the governor of the Bank of Canada.
I have in my hand a letter addressed to the Minister of Finance written by the governor of the bank and dated June 13, 1961. I should like to briefly quote from this letter to indicate that the minister's statement is not accurate from our point of view. That portion of this letter which I wish to read is as follows:
Efforts were made by the directors to arrange for discussion with you in order to be absolutely clear that you were aware that there was no issue of substance between the government and the bank or the government and myself prior to your request to me on May 30-to be sure that you knew that the bank felt bound to support government policies in so far as they had financial implications, as it had always done.
I now wish briefly, in that connection, to refer to a television broadcast some months ago on which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance appeared, because I think the issue was the question of high or low interest rates. I understand that program appeared nearly two years ago, at which time both these hon. gentlemen appealed to the public of Canada to dispose of their low interest bonds and accept higher interest government bonds. That does not indicate any concern with the question of low interest.
A reading of the correspondence that we have received from the governor of the Bank of Canada indicates that the government's primary and first concern is political, not economic, and that the statements made by the governor of the Bank of Canada were, as indicated in the correspondence and as the government indicated, "embarrassing". I think that was the substance of the complaint in the first instance.
The Minister of Finance has mentioned that there was a difference between the government and the governor of the Bank of Canada in respect to policies. I am not going to take the time of this house to go into that subject. The Leader of the Opposition has quoted to some extent to prove that was not an accurate statement, and we agree with that statement.
What does the government do according to this correspondence, according to the statement by the minister, and according to what we have read about this issue, in order to achieve its main purpose, to cover its political embarrassment because of the statements made by the governor of the Bank of Canada? It uses the smokescreen of a relatively unimportant issue, relatively unimportant in relation to the welfare of this country as a

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the unprecedented request by the government for the immediate resignation of the governor of the Bank of Canada and the circumstances related thereto.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I would be disposed to ask the house if it is prepared to grant leave, as this matter appears to come within the rule. The only reservation I have is that the government has indicated its intention to bring before the house a proposal which would permit debate on the definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the unprecedented request by the government for the immediate resignation of the governor of the Bank of Canada. Before I deal with the matter, perhaps I should hear hon. members.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief submission, not with respect to the importance of the matter itself but purely from the point of view of urgency of debate. I suggest that there might be three reasons why Your Honour would think the motion does not comply with that requirement of the rule. First, you permitted quite a far ranging discussion this morning, in which it is true that Your Honour did apply some limitation as to time, but with respect to which there was not much limitation as to range of debate. At least a full discussion was allowed within the context of the statement made by the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance, the Leader of the Opposition and the acting leader of the third party expressed, one assumes, the views of their parties in the house.
Second, the Minister of Finance announced today that the budget will be introduced on June 20. At that time, of course, there will be ample opportunity for debate, and that is just six days from now. It is, I suggest, difficult to see why the matter which has already been aired in the house would be so urgent of debate that the budget debate could not be awaited.
Third, Your Honour has yourself just made reference to the fact that the statement of the Minister of Finance indicated that legislation will be laid before parliament shortly to deal with this matter. I understand I have the authority of the minister to say that this will be as rapidly as satisfactory legislation can be drafted.
I would say, therefore, first that there has been quite a full airing of the matter here this morning; second, there is the budget debate; and third, legislation to amend the Bank of Canada Act itself will be introduced shortly, at which time a discussion can take place.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already had, though not in the course of debate, something to say on this matter. As you ruled, and quite properly, that a reply to a ministerial statement made on motions is not an occasion for debate, and as this matter is one of very grave importance and of the most immediate urgency, I have thought fitting to move this motion which will give to the members of the house an opportunity to discuss the whole question of the request by the government for the immediate resignation of the governor of the Bank of Canada and the circumstances related thereto.
It does not seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that anything the Minister of Finance said this morning removes the necessity for this kind of discussion at this time. It seems to me that it makes the urgency of such a discussion even greater than it was before the minister spoke. The minister made certain statements this morning which are in direct and complete contradiction to statements that have been made by the governor of the Bank of Canada in correspondence which has been made public. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is in the interests of getting this matter cleared up as quickly and as satisfactorily as possible that we should have a discussion.
It is even more important, I believe-and this is one of the reasons for asking for this discussion, as has been pointed out by the 90205-6-399J
Governor of Bank of Canada acting leader of the C.C.F. group-that the banking and commerce committee should be convened at once for this particular purpose. We have been asking for this during the session. We have been asking for it at a time when the minister has said there was no necessity for it, having given the impression that there was not any fundamental disagreement between the governor of the bank and the minister which would warrant a discussion before a committee. Surely after what the minister has said this morning the government itself would wish to convene the committee and would wish to get these matters cleared up so we can find out what are the facts. The governor could appear before this committee and be questioned about the statements he has made and the communications he has published. The minister would also, of course, wish to appear, and he could be questioned on these and related matters.
Now, I am aware of the fact that the minister said something this morning about the action which the government intends to take by way of submitting a proposal to this parliament. What the form of the proposal will be, we do not know. Perhaps it will be an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act, which I believe the minister has stated previously was the only way by which this kind of change could be made. The Minister of Justice seemed to confirm that statement this morning. It has also been suggested this might be done by order in council. We do not know when this action will be taken. We do not know when this measure, in whatever form it may be, will be submitted to the House of Commons. We do not know whether it will be done before the budget or after the budget.
One of the extraordinary circumstances surrounding this whole sorry business is that it has become tangled up with a budget which should have been introduced weeks ago. I believe I am fair in suggesting, from what the minister has said this morning, that there is a relationship between the bank's monetary and financial policy and government policy. I confess I was very surprised, indeed, this morning to hear the minister say that the government at no time-I hope he will correct me if I am misinterpreting or misquoting what he said-during the consideration of the budget and the negotiations leading up to the budget consulted the governor of the Bank of Canada. You would have thought, Mr. Speaker, during all these weeks of preparation designed, we have been told this morning, to introduce some pretty far reaching financial changes-because those changes were put forward as the basis of the difference between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the government-that the governor of the Bank of

Governor of Bank of Canada Canada would have been consulted. That is an extraordinary position, to say the least.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: No one said it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I hear from over there an interruption that no one said it. The minister said it this morning, and it is on the record. Perhaps my hon. friend who interrupted was not listening to the minister.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: He was too busy applauding.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
There are some other reasons why this discussion is most important and urgent and which should be put on the record. A very grave indictment indeed has been made against the governor. But interference and intervention in the affairs of the bank has been dealt with in communications which have been made public by the governor of the bank himself.
This morning the minister said that on May 30 the resignation of the governor of the bank was asked for or requested by the government through the minister. There is no use in the minister trying to take refuge in semantics and suggesting that parliament will decide, and all that he did was to approach the governor. The resignation of the governor was asked for on May 30 in circumstances which are outlined in some detail by the governor himself in public statements.
The minister said this morning that subsequent to that date, until the governor issued his statement yesterday he had no contact with the governor of the bank; no opportunity was given to him by the governor to discuss this matter further after May 30. That is the minister's statement, but let me read what the governor himself has said in a letter to the minister dated June 13, 1961. This letter deals not only with the relationship between the governor and the minister but also with the relationship between the board of directors of the bank and the government. I will read from this letter, Mr. Speaker:
Further to my letter of June 9 I have now had the benefit of three days' discussion with my board of directors, during which time several of them were in frequent communication by telephone with you.
The nature of some of these communications was made fairly clear by the minister this morning. The letter goes on:
It became apparent that there were no new arguments to be advanced why I should resign-
Mr. Speaker, I ask the house to take note of this, which is in direct contradiction to what the minister said this morning about the attitude of the directors of the bank over the preceding month. This letter goes on to state:

-and indeed the directors were all surprised and disturbed when they first heard that you had requested my resignation.
There is one contradiction that should be cleared up and can only be cleared up satisfactorily by a committee holding hearings on this matter, with evidence being taken. The letter goes on:
Many conversations were held both in the full board meeting and outside it, in the course of which I expressed the view that no valid case had been made for my resignation and that the board had no reason to expect it other than the fact that the government had asked for it.
We on this side of the house certainly have the right to take that position also, because there was no indication, in all the discussions we have had on this subject during this session, at any time by any representative of the government, let alone the Minister of Finance, that the relationship between the bank and the government was such that this action was likely to be taken. I refer to the action which was taken on May 30. Then Mr. Coyne's letter goes on:
Efforts were made by the directors to arrange for discussion with you-
That is, the Minister of Finance:
-in order to be absolutely clear that you were aware that there was no issue of substance between the government and the bank or the government and myself prior to your request to me on May 30-
In other words these very same directors, who according to the minister were already dissatisfied with the governor and were looking for his resignation-and these directors were characterized in those terms by the minister in this house this morning-attempted in recent days subsequent to May 30 to get in touch with the minister himself to find out if there was in fact any issue of substance between the government and the bank or the government and the governor. The letter goes on:
-to be sure that you knew-
That is, the minister knew:
-that the bank felt bound to support government policies in so far as they had financial Implications, as it had always done.
The governor himself said in his statement that it is the duty-and of course it is the duty-of the governor and the bank to support policies of the government. That doctrine had already been laid down emphatically on this side of the house and rejected by this government. Mr. Coyne in his statement and in this letter having said that it is the duty of the bank to support the policy of the government in the field in which both have jurisdiction, and that the bank has always done so, the Minister of Finance gets up this morning and denies that. I have not

his words before me, but he certainly gave that impression-and I am sure I am not misrepresenting what he said-when he said that far from supporting the policy of the government, the bank had been acting in contravention of the policies of the government and that that is the reason why these developments took place which required the government to intervene and request the resignation of the governor.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That was the main reason the minister gave this morning.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Yes, that was the main reason the minister gave this morning, though the governor indicated in one of his letters that apparently another reason was put forward, which was presumably to bring great pressure to bear on him. I refer to the question of his pension, and I will come to that a little later.
The letter goes on:
Each time your answer-
That is, the answer of the Minister of Finance:
Each time your answer was that the government had made up its mind and there was nothing to discuss.
In a matter of such fundamental importance which has shaken the confidence of the country in the relationship between the bank and the government, after the action taken by the minister on May 30 calling for the resignation of the governor of the bank, in reply to the efforts of the directors of the bank to get in touch with the minister and try to find out, if they could, what was behind all this, according to this letter the minister's reply was that the government had made up its mind and there was nothing to discuss. What a reflection, not only on the attitude of the minister but on the relationship between the minister and the bank. Mr. Coyne's letter goes on:
Finally this morning-
"This morning" is June 13, the date of this letter:
Finally this morning at about ten o'clock, after a further telephone talk with you, it was reported in open meeting of the board of directors that you had said to Mr. Hill that you would not consent to see me to discuss the matter.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
And the minister this morning said that Mr. Coyne did not make the effort. I am not quoting the minister's words exactly, but he said Mr. Coyne had not seen him and therefore the minister was surprised at the action taken by Mr. Coyne because he had no opportunity to discuss this matter. In this letter Mr. Coyne said that Mr. Hill, at the meeting of the board of directors, had told the
Governor of Bank of Canada board that the minister would not consent to see the governor to discuss the matter. What an attitude to take in regard to a matter of such very great importance.
So that I will not misquote the minister's words or be unfair to him in any way I would refer to the text of the minister's statement which, it has been called to my attention, was circulated this morning. That statement includes this; I had better read the paragraph: On May 30, on the instructions of the government, I asked Mr. Coyne to tender his resignation to the board of directors of the bank. I further asked that he do so before the regular board meeting to be held in Quebec on June 12 and 13, so that action might be taken by the board at its meeting on the resignation. I gave him an ample statement of the reasons for the course the government was following. The main reason was that the government was convinced that Mr. Coyne's continuation in office as governor of the Bank of Canada would stand in the way of the implementation of a comprehensive, sound and responsible economic program designed to raise the levels of employment and production in Canada. After an hour's discussion, he asked to be allowed to think the matter over. Presumably his published statement yesterday is his reply to the government's request.
Presumably his public statement yesterday was made after the minister refused to receive him, according to Mr. Coyne's own statement. Presumably also, his public statement yesterday was made after the minister had refused to see the board of directors of the Bank of Canada to discuss this matter with them. This is an almost unbelievable procedure. This is arrogance of a kind which is hard to contemplate, especially in the person of one who in the past used to talk so much in this house about the rights and privileges of parliament and of the individual. Then Mr. Coyne's letter goes on:
It was apparent to all that this closed the door- It is certainly apparent to anyone who reads this letter, if the facts are as stated, that it closed the door.
-and there were no avenues left by which useful communication could take place.
So the only thing left for Mr. Coyne to do was resign-or else. If a committee were set up to consider this matter we might be able to find out what the "or else" was. We do not know yet. The letter goes on:
I left the meeting to consider my position. In the face of your refusal to see me, I felt it incumbent upon me to issue a statement, of which you have a copy, setting forth very briefly my view of the situation which had been created by the action of the government in this matter.
I subsequently returned to the board meeting (which in the meantime had been dealing with affairs of the industrial development bank) and read to the directors the statement which I had made public at about 11 a.m.
The directors then decided to bring forward a resolution, which I understand had been discussed with you the day before, and which you had demanded that they should pass.

Governor of Bank of Canada
"Which you had demanded that they should pass". This is the statement made in Mi-. Coyne's letter. The letter goes on:
The text of the resolution proposed by Mr. Hill is as follows:
Mr. Hill, I take it, is one of the directors.
"Resolved that it is in the best interests of the Bank of Canada that the governor do immediately tender his resignation to the board of directors of the bank, and further that this action and decision on the part of the board has been taken after prolonged consideration and with regret."
I can understand a resolution of that kind being passed by the board of directors when the governor had reported to them that the minister who had requested his resignation would no longer see him and talk with him. It is clear that once a government takes an attitude of that kind toward a man in a position such as Mr. Coyne holds and refuses to talk with him or see him, his usefulness as governor of the bank is, to say the least seriously damaged. But let it also be said that this resolution which I have read out contained no reference of any kind to the conduct of the governor; no reference to the resignation being related in any way to the governor's inability to support government policies; no reference to the governor's conduct in any shape or form. The resolution merely says that because of this situation it is now in the best interests of the bank for the governor to resign. Then the letter goes on:
There was a discussion of the motion. One director spoke against it. I then put the motion to a vote and polled the directors individually. There was one director absent from the meeting. Of those present all voted in favour of the motion save one who registered his vote against.
After a negative response to my inquiry as to whether there was any further business to come before the meeting, the meeting of the board of directors of the Bank of Canada was terminated.
So much for that aspect of the situation. We shall have to get a lot more facts before we can accept the minister's interpretation of the relationship between the governor and himself referred to in this letter and referred to in the governor's statement in terms which the minister has contradicted this morning and which indeed, the minister himself has contradicted in this house previously. Because if, in fact, as I said a few moments ago, this situation was developing in which the bank was frustrating government policy, then surely it was the duty of the government to bring that situation before the House of Commons.
We introduced a motion on this subject some months ago. There was no suggestion at that time in the discussion, either by the minister or anyone else on the government side, that this bad situation was developing. We asked questions as recently as May 30,

the day on which the resignation was requested. There was no indication then from the minister of what he now tells us is the real difficulty, the fact that the governor was frustrating, as the minister says, the policies of the government.
What is even more extraordinary, the minister now says the governor is impeding the carrying out of the government's new, expansionist policy; the expansionist policy, incidentally, of a government which introduced the conversion loan and has done so much to establish the highest interest rates in our history. But there is to be a new, expansionist policy, presumably to be embodied in the long delayed budget, and it would not be possible, according to the government, for the governor to work with the government in the implementation of this policy concerning which they did not talk to the governor at all in the discussions leading up to the budget. In the minister's own words:
The government's policy is expansionist, aimed at the creation of more trade, more production and more jobs. The policies advocated by Mr. Coyne are restrictionist.
If this is a fact, why did we not hear something about it in the house over the past weeks and months? If this is the way the government feels about Mr. Coyne, why was this matter not brought into the House of Commons where we could have discussed it together with the relationship between the government and the bank? The fact is that this is an ex post facto rationalization of the mess into which the government has got itself by its arbitrary and arrogant behaviour. If in fact the governor of the Bank of Canada could not work in harmony with the government-and he has denied this; he has denied, also, that he did not support its policy and denied that he would not support it-if the governor could not do that, then of course, he should resign. We have been saying that since this session began. Responsibility in these matters, we have repeatedly stated, belongs to the government, and if they feel that the governor is taking action and making speeches and interfering with monetary and fiscal policy then, of course, it is the duty of the governor to resign. That doctrine was laid down by Graham Towers, and it is a doctrine to which we subscribe. But that is not the situation with which we were confronted this session. The minister has denied the validity of that doctrine in the past and said that monetary policy is the responsibility of the Bank of Canada and we have no share in that responsibility at all. In other words the government may interfere with pension arrangements in the bank but not with monetary policy.

When we challenged that doctrine here the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance rejected our challenge and insisted that what the governor did in this field was the governor's responsibility, and that what the governor said in his speeches was also the governor's responsibility, because this is a free country and he should be allowed to speak as a free man if he wished. We now learn from these documents, and I think the minister confirmed this fact this morning, although I am not sure, that he did indeed intervene with Mr. Coyne at one stage back in March, and told him that his speeches were embarrassing the government. Presumably that was after the speech made by Mr. Coyne in New York. I think I am right in saying that.
At that time, when Mr. Coyne was approached and told that his speeches were embarrassing the government, the minister got up in this house and said that he was a free man and could say what he wished. Now the minister informs us that this was the beginning of the end of Mr. Coyne. Mr. Coyne himself refers to this episode in his communication, and apparently admitted the right of the minister to quarrel with his speeches. However, he said in one of his letters that since that time he has made no public statement which could conceivably be of embarrassment to the government. He has also gone on to say that whatever policy, monetary or fiscal, the government sees fit to put into effect, he and the bank should support it or, naturally, he as governor should resign. He had no reason until May 30 to believe that this situation had developed to the point where his resignation could suddenly and shockingly be asked for by the Minister of Finance.
Mr. Speaker, that is the way this government does business. They allow problems to roll on and on, with the hope that something will happen by which they will disappear; and when the problems become crises, as this one has become a crisis, they take this kind of panic action based on political expediency in the hope of rushing something through which will do away with the crisis.
In this situation there is something else involved which relates to the board of directors, a question which is very much in the public mind, and which has certain sinister significance, namely the change in the pension position. The impression has been created that somehow or other the governor of the bank took action on his own in February, 1960 which increased his pension position, or that he should have prevented the action being taken. An impression of that kind has been given in respect to either negative or positive action on his part, and

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house took recess at one o'clock the question had arisen as to the incredulity or otherwise of a situation where a meeting of the board of directors of the Bank of Canada could be held at which important decisions were taken and those decisions not be brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance. The minister has said that that was the situation and of course I accept his word, but it certainly is astonishing to say the least that in a situation of this kind in those circumstances the minister would not know what was going on; and a year and a half later would raise the issue with the governor.
It is true the deputy minister was not at this meeting; I believe he was at a funeral. The assistant deputy minister was there and therefore the situation undoubtedly is, from our point of view, one that inspires astonishment if not incredulity.
This whole sorry business, Mr. Speaker, is depressing evidence of the unprecedented break-down in relation between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance. This break-down is disturbing to parliament; it is certainly disturbing to the business and financial community in Canada, and indeed abroad, and it is bad for business confidence in this country at a time when such confidence is so important.
The minister has emphasized that this has been developing over the months and the reason he had to take this kind of action on May 30 was that the governor of the Bank of Canada was standing in the way of an expansionist policy of the government, and that this had been clear. He referred to two previous budgets to show the difference between them. This brings us back a couple of years. While it may be clear to the minister now that the Bank of Canada was adopting a restrictionist policy at the time when the government wished to put into effect an expansionist policy in the monetary and economic field, it was not clear to the minister on February 21 of this year. That was the day when we on this side of the house criticized some of the policies of the Bank of Canada because in our view they were restrictionist. Did the minister agree with us then and give us an assurance that something would be done? Not at all. If hon. members

will turn to page 2265 of Hansard they will see where the minister challenged our criticism and put statistics on the record to show that the Bank of Canada's monetary policy had been expansionist. What happened between February 21 and June 13 to cause the minister to change his mind so completely in this matter and to use his changed position to justify the action taken on May 30?
It is interesting to note that in that same debate the minister had this to say about the responsibilities of the government in these matters, as reported at page 2264 of Hansard:
I made my statement with reference to over-all financial policy in Canada. I do not think there is anything in that statement which ought to be interpreted as supporting the thesis put forward by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday that under the provisions enacted by parliament with respect to the Bank of Canada Act, the government has power to direct the Bank of Canada or to call upon the Bank of Canada to observe a position of responsibility to the government as such, rather than to parliament.
In other words, on February 21 the minister said that he and the government have no authority "to call upon the Bank of Canada to observe a position of responsibility to the government", and yet on May 30 he calls in the governor of the Bank of Canada and says, "I want your resignation".
Let me also put on the record the proper doctrine, the doctrine which has always been accepted until recent months, on this matter of relationship between the government and the bank. I would refer to the banking and commerce committee of 1954 when the minister of today, a private member of the opposition of that day, was questioning the governor of the Bank of Canada of that day. He asked Mr. Towers a question on this matter and he received this reply. I quote from page 715 of the proceedings and evidence of the committee of that year. Mr. Towers said:
The government, of course, either through the deputy minister of finance, who is a member of the board and of the executive committee, or through quite frequent conversations between the governor and the Minister of Finance, is always aware of what the Bank of Canada is doing.
I wonder whether these quite frequent conversations which, in the opinion of the previous governor, were so desirable and necessary, have been going on in the last year or two between the minister and the present governor? If not, why not?
Then the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) asked this question:
For instance, in 1948 and in 1951, when you urged the chartered banks to restrict credit, was that advice given without the government first having been consulted by you?
90205-6-400
Governor of Bank of Canada
Mr. Towers replied:
The government would be aware that we were going to have the conversations. They would be aware, at least through the deputy minister.
Then the following exchange occurred:
Q. And having offered no objection, I suppose one could say they were parties to it, at least in the sense that they did not interfere?
A. Yes, because automatically, indeed, they must be parties to everything the central bank does unless they signify to the contrary.
Presumably, the hon. member for Eglinton was happy at that time to hear that doctrine expressed by the governor of the bank. It is certainly a quite startling contradiction of the doctrine he put forward this morning. I recognize, Mr. Speaker, we all recognize, that the views of the governor, even his right to express those views, are often controversial. This has been the case in respect of some statements that he, the governor, has made in the last year or two. These views have been questioned by many and they have been supported by many. Indeed, in this house members on this side have questioned the validity of some of the views put forward by the governor of the Bank of Canada. But what was the attitude of the government when we took that position? In all the discussions when we were the ones who were questioning some of these views there was not a word from the government either in defence or in criticism of the governor of the bank but rather a shrugging of the shoulders and the indication that monetary policy had nothing to do with them.
Mr. Coyne's views may have been criticized and they may or they may not be in dispute, but I do not think it is in dispute that he is a man of high principle and integrity who is devoted to the public service and to his duty and is uninfluenced by unworthy considerations. Therefore, whatever we may think about the validity of some parts of his economic doctrine, surely he should not be persecuted or victimized or misrepresented for stating his views when the Minister of Finance says that the governor has every right as a free Canadian so to do.
In the minister's statement this morning, the text of which I have now had the opportunity to read, the Minister of Finance had this to say:
As I indicated earlier, it is not my intention to comment in detail on Mr. Coyne's statement. I should like, however, to make two observations. First, by referring to a "mysterious and alarming" program which the government is contemplating, Mr. Coyne may have left a certain false impression with the public.

That is in quotes, "mysterious and alarming" program. I say that by using

Governor of Bank of Canada those words in that context the minister has indeed left a false impression as to what Mr. Coyne said. I have a copy of Mr. Coyne's statement before me, as the minister must have had before him, and here is what Mr. Coyne said:
The Minister of Finance has suggested to me that another reason the government wanted me out of the way was that they were preparing certain programs which were apparently thought to be of such character that I would oppose them.
He mentioned "certain programs" and that is the only expression he used. Then Mr. Coyne went on to say in his statement:
This mysterious and alarming suggestion has not been clarified.
"Mysterious and alarming" were the words used by Mr. Coyne to describe the suggestion that he would be opposing the program of the government. The minister takes those words, puts them in front of the word "program" and thereby certainly misrepresents what Mr. Coyne said. It is obvious on the face of it, of course. The minister said:
... by referring to a "mysterious and alarming" program-
Mr. Coyne made no such reference and the minister owes it to him to withdraw that statement. The minister went on to say in his statement, from the text of which I now quote:
Perhaps the best way to dispel this impression is for me to say at once that Mr. Coyne has not been told of the contents of the forthcoming budget-
This is the governor of the Bank of Canada and the budget has been under consideration for many months.
-and, therefore, has no right whatsoever to express views about it. Second, Mr. Coyne has asserted that he has been given no indication of disagreement with his views on economic policy. In my last two budgets and in various other public statements, it has been clear for some time that there have been major differences of opinion with the frequently expressed views of the governor on economic matters.
If there have been major differences of opinion of that kind dating back for two budgets, why did the minister not get up in the house and state these differences of opinion? The minister said that finally his patience was exhausted. What patience? How often has the minister discussed these matters with the governor of the Bank of Canada in an effort to clear up these differences of opinion? According to the governor in his statement, the minister refused to see him after May 30. The fact is that it is clear on the face of it and confirmed by what has happened since May 30 that there has been a failure on the part of the government to establish adequate communication with the bank. There has been a failure to consult,

to advise and to discuss. Obviously there has been a break-down in this important relationship, the result of which was the request from the Minister of Finance on May 30 for the governor of the bank to resign immediately on the ground that there is a fundamental difference of policy with regard to economic and financial matters between the governor and the government. Here is what Mr. Coyne has to say about that. Let the minister deal with this statement.
I may add that at no time has the government expressed disagreement with the operations of the Bank of Canada under my management, either in the field of monetary policy, or in those fields in which we act solely as agents and under the instructions of the Minister of Finance, namely, in debt management and in operation of the exchange fund. There has likewise never been any occasion on which the Bank of Canada has failed to co-operate, so far as it was concerned in the matter, in support of government policy. In financial matters we have always loyally played our part in carrying out positive government policies.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, the only way we will get down to the facts of the matter is to have a committee before which Mr. Coyne can appear and the minister can appear. Various explanations have been given outside the house, of course, to explain this crisis, this whole sorry business. Mr. John Meyer of the Montreal Gazette had this to say in his editorial this morning:
One St. James street source put it this way:
"Mr. Coyne isn't winning any votes for Mr. Diefenbaker so Mr. Coyne has to go."
That is another variation of the "heads will roll" approach of the government. Mr. John Meyer also had this to say in another article:
It was, as Mr. Coyne says, "A slander upon my own integrity which I cannot ignore or accept."
This refers to the pension.
This will be how the public as well will interpret the government's action. In seeking to discredit Mr. Coyne, the government has succeeded only in discrediting itself.

I would welcome any serious interruption by the hon. and learned financial pundit on my left. The issue before us, Mr. Speaker, is very important but a very simple one. If the government ask parliament to remove the governor of the Bank of Canada because the governor has in fact prevented them from implementing their monetary and financial policies, and if that can be established through a parliamentary inquiry, then, of course, we on this side would support his removal. That has been the relationship we have put forward all along and we would support it now. That has been the relationship, that has been the doctrine which has been opposed by the government.

If in fact the government can do this, if they can establish that they have been so opposed, the governor of the Bank of Canada should resign. We would support that course in those circumstances because we believe that our system of responsible government would necessitate such a course. We do not think that any public servant should be in a position where he can prevent a democratic government from implementing its policies. But, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has not made that case. Indeed all his observations in the last six months in the house challenge the validity of that case.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that most of us will agree that we are debating this issue under a very great handicap, namely the lack of adequate information. We have not had a budget brought down as yet, and until we have had a look at the budget we cannot really understand what is meant by a possibility that the governor of the Bank of Canada may have serious reservations about the contents of the budget. Also, we have not been told what the proposed legislation is going to contain. I assume, since the minister mentioned legislation, that the government is contemplating the Bank of Canada Act. This is a move of great significance, and the information as to the intended legislation as well as the contents of the budget would enable us to debate the issue before us now in a much more intelligent manner.
I feel that the government has been negligent in not making this information available to us. However, I believe that at least all of us in the opposition would readily agree that the whole government is in a mess. The government did not expect the governor of the Bank of Canada to have the guts that history has now proven he has. They did not expect he would release to the public the information that he has released. In looking over this whole affair, it is obvious to me that "John" has won out over "Don". It 90205-6-400J
Governor of Bank of Canada appears that there is going to be the introduction of a new attitude on the part of the government toward Canadian economic problems.
The government, of course, is looking for an out. They remember only too well what happened the last time a Conservative government was unable to meet the needs of the Canadian people. This Conservative government, under the late Mr. Bennett, made a deathbed repentance in 1935. I believe the intention is to repeat that deathbed repentance by the introduction of some rather large, comprehensive new programs in order to help the people forget all the disappointments of the years since 1957. The government has to find an individual who can be used as a scapegoat. It is obvious to me at least that the governor of the Bank of Canada is intended to be the scapegoat so that the members who support the government will be able to pillory him during the next election campaign. I believe it is for this reason that the pension arrangements have been introduced into the argument.
We are not, in any way, defending the $25,000 a year pension. However, the government knows very well that private banks retire their governors on a much higher pension than even the $25,000, and at least one other civil servant, namely the head of the Canadian National Railways, would be entitled to an even higher pension than the one the board of directors arranged for the retiring governor of the Bank of Canada. In addition, I have read the act very carefully and I find no possibility of the government having any kind of voice in determining the level of the pensions of ex-employees of the Bank of Canada.
The pension matter was mentioned by the governor in his release to the press on June 13 last. If one reads this release very carefully, one is almost inclined to be a little suspicious that he was, in effect, advised that if he would be a nice boy and sneak away quietly the government might consider leaving his pension at $25,000 a year.

speechtext: That is utterly untrue.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
However, Mr. Coyne is a very responsible man, and Mr. Coyne also relates his responsibility to the board of directors. He says in paragraph 1:
He said the government-
The "he" refers to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming).
-were considering what action to take in the matter of the pension, had not yet come to a decision, and wanted my resignation before they came to a decision.

Governor of Bank of Canada
The only conclusion I can come to from reading that part is that he was, in effect, told to be a nice little boy and we-the government-will not be overly harsh with you in the matter of reducing your pension. I do not believe the pension could be reduced without an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act.
There is another matter that alarms me. There is no indication that anywhere along the line a serious difference of opinion existed between the board of directors and the governor. We hear now that last night, by an almost unanimous vote, the board of directors has asked for Mr. Coyne's resignation. I believe the minister owes it to this house to inform us as to why there has been an apparent change of heart on the part of the board of directors of the Bank of Canada. I, for one, would like to know how many consultations the minister has had with how many members of the board on the matter of taking the action that the board took last night when they finally asked for the resignation of the governor. In all the correspondence we have been allowed to see, there has been no indication that at any time the board of directors was dissatisfied or displeased with the work of the governor. However, we find that at the very crucial moment the board of directors asked for the resignation of this man.
I agree at once that the Bank of Canada must work in harmony with the government of Canada. I believe that is essential. The Minister of Finance, for a very good reason, is the only owner, on behalf of all the people of Canada, of this institution known as the Bank of Canada, and that would not be so were the intention not that the Bank of Canada should work in harmony with the government of the day. I had always assumed that they were working in harmony and this revelation is rather surprising to us. In the past there has not been any appearance of a conflict. I had always considered Mr. Coyne and the minister to be good, true blue Conservatives when it came to financial matters. I would like to indicate that in my opinion a conflict did not appear to exist in previous years. Reading from page 1063 of Hansard of November 13, 1957, the Hon. James Sinclair the then member for Coast-Capilano, asked the minister:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Actually it is a repetition of a question he was asked last Monday in Oakville, which he refused to answer on the ground that he could not answer it outside the House of Commons. Since he is now inside the House of Commons I should like to ask him, has there been a clash of opinions between the Bank of Canada and the government on economic policy?


The answer of the minister was:
I am not aware of anything that could be called a clash.
Mr. Sinclair asked another question:
A supplementary question. Does that mean the Minister of Finance is now in accord with the policy of the Bank of Canada which he called an unhappy legacy earlier this session?
The minister replied:
The expression "unhappy legacy" does not apply only to what the hon. gentleman has lust mentioned. There are a good many things in the unhappy legacy to which that expression ought to apply. When the time comes to deal with any questions of policy in the house I can assure the hon. gentleman that they will be dealt with fully.
I should like to underline the last word "fully". The minister has never on any occasion, in the years that have intervened since November 13, 1957, indicated that there was the slightest clash of opinion between himself and the governor of the Bank of Canada.
If there is a basic conflict, as the minister now seems to contend, I believe parliament is entitled to know what that basic conflict is and I hope, at least, the minister when he replies later on in the afternoon is going to be much more explicit as to the basic conflict than he was in his rather bland assertions this morning.
I had always assumed the two men were both excellent Conservatives. I realize, of course, that the governor of the bank was not appointed by this minister, but he was appointed by the equally Tory minded minister who preceded him. The minister mentions one possible clash. He complains-and these were his words-of Mr. Coyne's rigid attitude on the maintenance of high interest rates, as one example.
I can remember very well that the two men who led the campaign in Canada in favour of higher interest rates were our present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and our Minister of Finance. I have reference to their television appearance on the subject of the bond conversion loan.

speechtext: Ridiculous.
