We now realize that interest rates in Canada are on an average a number of percentage points higher than they were at the time when this government assumed office, and I feel this government must assume responsibility for that. It is in very poor taste, to say the least, for them, after four years in office to now all of a sudden be blaming the governor of the Bank of Canada for pursuing

a policy which they claim was in contradiction to government policy, in maintaining a rigid attitude on the maintenance of high interest rates. I believe the government cannot successfully escape its responsibility in this regard.
I notice also, in connection with the minister's attempt to blame the governor of the bank for high interest rates, that as reported at page 3093 of Hansard for April 27, 1959, the minister had this to say:
I think I should begin this reply, Mr. Speaker, by a reference to what actually has occurred in the money market of Canada. We have had a money market in this country now for approximately the last four years. Money markets are not greatly different from commodity markets in this respect, that they are governed, not entirely but very largely, by the law of supply and demand. Obviously if the demand is large in relation to supply the return on borrowings must be larger_
Yet today we are told the rigid policy of the governor of the Bank of Canada has been responsible for these high interest rates. At page 3095 the minister went on:
Then, the Bank of Canada, on November 1, 1956 set its rates in terms of a formula attached to the treasury bill rate.
Then a little later on:
Let us bear in mind that the government of Canada does not establish the Bank of Canada rate.
He continued:
The Bank of Canada, by an act of the parliament of Canada, is responsible for monetary policy, and this bank rate, as it is called, is set each week by the Bank of Canada in the exercise of its statutory powers.
This policy that was begun on November 1, 1956, was for the Bank of Canada rate to be automatically tied to the current rate payable on treasury bills. The Bank of Canada, as of that November 1, no longer determined the rate excepting that it attached an increase of a certain constant amount to the yield realized whenever the government offered treasury bills.
On the problem of tight money, at page 1444 of Hansard of February 27, 1959, the minister had this to say. I asked the minister this question:
X should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance, of which I have not given him notice. Is the minister in a position to inform the house as to the effect on the Canadian economy of yesterday's announcement by the Bank of Canada of a new discount rate of 4.32 per cent, and does he still feel as he did on February 13 that this represents a fluctuation within a not very wide range?
The minister replied:
The rate on treasury bills over the past two weeks is approximately what it was when the Liberal government went out of office.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) interjected:
Tight money.
Governor of Bank of Canada
I then asked a supplementary question:
I should like to follow that with a supplementary question. Is the government taking any measures to establish a rediscount rate independent of the weekly offerings of treasury bills, or is this government now endorsing the tight money policy of the former government?
The minister proceeded to give me a considerable lecture, and I am getting used to them by now. He replied:
The hon. gentleman, if he is acquainted with what has been happening in the money markets of this continent, must be aware that interest rates have been rising rapidly in the United States. This has had an inevitable effect on interest rates in this country.
Today the minister is blaming the governor of the Bank of Canada for the unduly high levels of interest rates that have been prevailing. In my opinion the minister has been very long in arriving at this conclusion. If he had accepted his responsibilities as the sole owner of the Bank of Canada on behalf of the people of Canada, if this actually was happening the minister should have warned the Canadian people and should have taken action many years ago along the line he is now proposing. He would have saved the people of Canada a lot of the needless misery that unemployment has caused our country. The minister cannot rightfully claim that the governor of the Bank of Canada was responsible.
The minister further claims that the governor is not aware of the contents of the proposed budget. This sounds almost unbelievable, and had the minister not made that claim I would even label it as fantastic. Does the minister mean to say that before a budget is brought down-and I know the minister has no research facilities in his department-exceeding $5 billion-

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Seven billion dollars.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
-the effects of that budget are not called to the attention of the responsible people in the Bank of Canada? If that is the case, I say that the minister is completely unworthy of presenting a budget in this house. That is one of the purposes of the Bank of Canada, and if the minister is taxing the people of Canada to the tune of almost $6 billion a year without prior consultation with the bank on these matters I think he has been most derelict in discharging the duties assigned to him.
I am of the opinion that Mr. Coyne likely knows much more about the contents of the budget which is to come down than the minister is aware. I know the minister made his claim honestly, believing it to be true. However, in the release to the press which he prepared Mr. Coyne said this:

Governor of Bank of Canada
The Minister of Finance has suggested to me that another reason the govermnent wanted me out of the way was that they were preparing certain programs which were apparently thought to be of such a character that I would oppose them.
Later on, he said:
It is for the government to disclose to the public what it is they are planning to do.
I think that is so. I think it is for the government to disclose to the public what they are planning to do. However, the governor, who is an honourable man, thought it would be way out of line for him to tell the public about any action which the government planned to take. He says:
It is for the government to disclose to the public what it is they are planning to do. I have never opposed government policy and do not wish to do so. It is conceivable at some stage and in some circumstances it would be the duty of the governor of the bank to resign on an important question of principle or policy.
Yet the government wants Mr. Coyne out of the way before the budget is brought down. If relations are as the minister described them as being this morning, I think the honourable course would be to bring down the budget and then to see whether Mr. Coyne would carry out his pledge to work with the government in a co-operative spirit as I understand he has repeatedly assured the government he is anxious to do. The statement which I have just read is an indication that if Mr. Coyne found himself honestly unable to support the government in its proposal then, in his opinion, it would be his duty to hand in his resignation. I see nothing dishonourable in the course proposed throughout this controversy by Mr. Coyne, though I can find much that is reprehensible, to say the least, in this obvious attempt by the government to rid itself of the governor of the Bank of Canada without the public knowing anything about it. It is apparent that an effort was made to persuade Mr. Coyne to fold his tent like the Arabs and move away. I think the government has made a miscalculation inasmuch as they did not expect that Mr. Coyne would appeal to the public with regard to the methods being used by the government. I believe Mr. Coyne knows much more about the budget than the minister supposes and that he has very strong views on what is contained in it.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
On a point of order, the hon. member repeatedly suggests that Mr. Coyne knows all about the budget. We have the assurance of the Minister of Finance that the budget is still locked in his own brain. Regardless of party we all respect the Minister of Finance, and I suggest that this

repeated allegation, which is in direct contradiction to the minister's statement, is almost an insult and that it should be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The hon. member who raises this point of order may recall what has been said earlier. He may remember that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam did accept unreservedly the statement of the minister that as far as he knew, within his knowledge, Mr. Coyne did not know about the budget. The other statement is, to my mind, a different statement and I do not think the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam can properly be asked to withdraw it.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I believe the government owes it to parliament and to the country at this time to disclose the nature of the major moves which are being contemplated by the administration because we cannot adequately assess this situation which now faces us without that information. It may be the government is contemplating a billion dollar deficit in an attempt to win an early election. It may be the government is contemplating the sale of crown corporations-I notice that Mr. Coyne refers to these corporations-and thus may be linked with the announcement of the Prime Minister that the next election will be based on socialism versus free enterprise. Or, it may have something to do with the proposed disposal of mortgages, and over a billion dollars worth of them are held by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. If it were possible to sell these successfully I can see how the government might embark on an ambitious vote catching program without having to increase taxation or, necessarily, incurring a deficit. I should like to refer to one of the statements made by the minister in his speech this morning. He said:
At this stage I must confine myself to placing before the house the essential facts virtually none of which appear in that statement.
"That statement" refers obviously to the release issued by Mr. Coyne. I should like to ask the minister to tell us exactly which of the statements made by the governor of the Bank of Canada he denies. I should like to have a list of the statements made by Mr. Coyne and contained in this three-page press release of June 13 that are being denied by the minister. More specifically I should like to have the minister reconcile the reports of the meeting which was held last night in Quebec city when the board of directors asked the governor to resign. The governor, in a letter dated June 13 addressed to the minister had this to say in the final paragraph:
After a negative response to my inquiry as to whether there was any further business to come

before the meeting, the meeting of the board of directors of the Bank of Canada was terminated.
Yet the minister, in his monstrous attempts to cast reflections on the integrity of the governor of the Bank of Canada, reported that Mr. Coyne took an altogether different action. On page 3 of what the minister had to tell us this morning this version appears:
Mr. Coyne polled the directors. The resolution was carried by a vote of nine to one. Mr. Coyne did not vote. Having declared the motion carried, Mr. Coyne then immediately adjourned the meeting.
In doing so, he not only defied the formally expressed wish of the board that he should resign immediately in the interests of the bank, he made it impossible for them to proceed to consider what action might be taken in the face of this defiance.
Obviously Mr. Coyne has given us a wrong report of what happened, or the minister has misunderstood the report of what actually happened and conveyed the misunderstanding, through his own interpretation of what took place. However, the allegation contained in this discrepancy is a very important one to Mr. Coyne and to all of us who are interested in accurate reporting and the maintenance of the reputations of the individuals concerned.
Mr. Coyne reports that after the vote was taken and recorded he asked whether there was any other business to come before the board. No one said anything so the meeting was adjourned. The minister has indicated that Mr. Coyne made it impossible for the board to proceed with any other business that was before it at the time. There is a contradiction there of a very serious nature.
I hope the minister, in the interest of accuracy, and I know he does wish to be accurate, will clear this matter up. I hope he is able to tell us that Mr. Coyne wrongly reported what took place at the meeting, or that he was in error, or that one of his advisers supplied him with wrong advice, because I cannot imagine the minister deliberately making a statement with such implications. He either made the statement knowing that he was not accurately reporting what did take place, or was unaware of the fact that he was in error.
After blaming Mr. Coyne for his rigid attitude in maintaining high interest rates, the minister goes on to blame him for other things. Before I resume my seat I should like to make it very clear that we have always assumed that Mr. Coyne and the minister were working together in harmony. We have had no indication, either in the policies of this government or in the statements made by the governor of the Bank of Canada, that there was a basic conflict in the attitudes of the Bank of Canada and the government of Canada. However, we do claim that the
Governor of Bank of Canada two must work in harmony. If the minister can supply us with adequate reason, substantiated by facts and not by mere assertions, that the governor of the Bank of Canada has been working against the announced policies of this government then, of course, we should have no alternative but to support the demand of the government that the governor of the Bank of Canada resign because we still contend, in spite of everything the minister has said over the years, that this government is responsible for the monetary policies of Canada and it cannot evade that responsibility.
I am pleased to note that in at least one respect this government has now returned to that attitude which was once held by the minister himself when he was in opposition. However, I regret very much that this whole situation has to be part of an election campaign, and that one of our most highly esteemed federal civil servants, even though he was a Tory, has to have his name blackened and smeared by a government which is so ruthlessly desperate to win re-election it feels it must resort to measures of this kind.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about this very serious subject. I suggest it is serious in view of the fact that I have never before seen the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) so het up as he was today.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You ain't seen nothing yet.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I suggest to the Leader of the Opposition that he get his facts straight, following the example set by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) who, I understand, took history lectures from him at university in the 1920's.
I should like to draw attention to the statement the Leader of the Opposition made regarding Mr. Jack Bryden, who was a director of the Bank of Canada, and the implication therein contained. That hon. member was brought up sharply by the Minister of Finance who stated that he knew with assurance that Mr. Bryden resigned from the Bank of Canada on his own initiative due to the fact that his other duties were very heavy.
I have known Jack Bryden for at least 30 years. He is a fine, upright, brilliant economist and the head of one of the large life insurance companies. I have very high regard for him, and think it was very small on the part of the Leader of the Opposition to cast the aspersion which he did, on the reputation of Mr. Bryden.
Another example of the type of statement the Leader of the Opposition makes without having checked the facts, was presented this morning when the Minister of Finance informed him that the deputy minister was not

Governor of Bank of Canada at the meeting of directors when the change in pension was made. The Leader of the Opposition then corrected his statement. I suggest he should have lectured in mathematics at the university, a little more exacting subject than history.
I have had special interest in the Bank of Canada for a good number of years because, in 1934, when that great Canadian, R. B. Bennett, incorporated the Bank of Canada as a private enterprise, the shares were sold to Canadians. I had one share certificate which I cherished but it was redeemed because of the policies of the last Liberal government. I can remember the year 1935 as though it was last night, when Mackenzie King went out on the hustings. I attended a meeting on College street in Toronto when Hugh Plaxton the Liberal candidate announced the policy of the Liberal party, saying that if that party was elected it would nationalize the Bank of Canada. That government, of course, was elected and did nationalize the bank. For that reason I suggest we can now lay the blame on the opposition side of this house for the troubles we are having.
Mr. R. B. Bennett established the Bank of Canada originally on the same basis as the Bank of England, and I wish it was still that way because I am sure we would not have had the problems with which we are faced today.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: We are back to old R. B. again.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes, sir.

speechtext: Get on your motorcycle and ride away.

I should think hon. members would hesitate to bring personalities into this debate, particularly in reference to the presidents and heads of our crown corporations. I believe it is quite unfair for any hon. member to engage in personalities in this house in respect of individuals who find themselves in positions in which they cannot defend themselves. I refer particularly to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who, with his flair for publicity, stood up and demanded that Donald Gordon resign. I was very sorry to hear some of our own party members concur with that statement because I do not agree with that type of practice at all. If we intend to have good men at the head of our corporations it ill behooves us to stand up in this house and verbally cut them down. We certainly cannot expect to build up the morale or prestige

of those organizations by appointing individuals and then immediately criticizing them.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: What about the governor?

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
How many members have risen in their places in this house-and this applies particularly to the hon. member for Port Arthur-and criticized Donald Gordon for not making the railroad pay? When Donald Gordon as head of the Canadian National Railways has endeavoured to put some efficiency into the operation of the railways how many times has the hon. member for Port Arthur and others opposed it? Time after time they have done this. When the C.P.R. lays off men because they have no work for them, or tries to eliminate costs, we do not hear about it in this house, but every time the C.N.R. does it we hear about it. I defy any man to manage the Canadian National Railways on the basis on which we are trying to operate it.
In the late 1920's Sir Henry Thornton was president of the Canadian National Railways and there were kicks about his methods of running the railroad. I defy any man-

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The Tories cut his throat as well.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I hesitate to engage in personalities with respect to the governor of the Bank of Canada but the opposition have asked for it. I support the Minister of Finance in the action he has taken.
Let us take a look at this Mr. Coyne. Who is he? He graduated from the university of Manitoba in 1931. He was a Rhodes scholar. I commend him for that. He took up law and was engaged in the practice of law from 1934 to 1938, and then lie got a job as secretary in the Bank of Canada. I believe he was in the armed forces for a couple of years during the war. He came back and became deputy governor of the bank. But what experience did the man have to operate a bank? I do not set myself up as an authority on the operation of a central bank but I was engaged in finance and I do know that two and two make four. I have sometimes wondered in the last year, when I have read Mr. Coyne's speeches, whether he knows that two and two make four. The first speech I read was the one he made in Calgary when he said we were spending far beyond our means. Well, he is the governor of the Bank of Canada and he had a certain amount of control over things. Consumer buying had gone up; consumer credit had expanded and he could have controlled that very easily. He should not have waited until 1960 to start his program.

Another point he made had to do with foreign investment coming into Canada. He said that if we stopped it and lived within our means it would help the unemployment situation. Well, gentlemen, I was at the other place-

I wish the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) could have been there to hear what the governor had to say, because I as the chairman of the banking and commerce committee would have liked to have Mr. Coyne appear before our committee-

I will give you the answer. After going to the Senate committee on manpower and listening to the deliberations and Mr. Coyne's cure for unemployment-he said he had all the plans, he had all the solutions for this and that-I came to a different conclusion. Let hon. members ask the senators how much they got out of him; and they were not Conservative senators. The first thing I took exception to after we were elected was his statement when he was accused of operating under a tight money policy. We came in, in 1957. I used the statement because I know I was right. The statement said we were operating the Bank of Canada on a tight money policy. The governor denied it. I understand that the Liberals had some doubts about Mr. Coyne. As a matter of fact, I have heard that they laid a great deal of the blame for losing the 1957 election on the tight money policy.
This morning the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) was disturbed. I think the reason he was disturbed was that he would have liked, and those on the other side would have liked, to see Mr. Coyne continue in his position so that his policies might help to defeat us.

speechtext: I do not know that we have been so slow.

speechtext:
I think that if we had had Mr. Coyne before the banking and commerce committee we would have further advertised what the Liberals have been advertising all over the world, namely that conditions in Canada are not good. They have enjoyed the gloom and this is another example. The hon. member for Essex East has been trying every day to get the governor of the Bank of Canada before the committee in order further to depress foreign credit. I should like to point out to hon. members the danger of weakening our foreign credit. We need the money from foreign investments in this country to develop our resources and we cannot get along without it. I know because I was in the investment business for a long time.
I know the attitude of United States investors toward Canada. It has taken a long time to build up and establish the fine credit we have in foreign countries. I think speeches such as those delivered by Mr. Coyne last year have undone a great deal of the good done in past years.
He has made reference to foreign investment in Canada. This foreign investment did not really start until 1949, when the foreign exchange control regulations were lifted and foreign capital came in. It came here because Canada was a safe haven for investment for people all over the world. I recall being in Switzerland in 1951 and talking to the bankers there. The reason they were so inclined to invest in Canada was that they knew us, that we were honest and that we had no exchange regulations.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: And at that time we had a good government.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The good government referred to is the government that is responsible. They saw what was happening. It started in 1949 and continued thereafter and if they thought it was such a bad thing they could have done something to remedy the situation.
There is something else which arouses a great deal of fear in my mind with respect to Mr. Coyne and that is his judgment with regard to foreign investment. In one of his statements he said that in companies in Canada for which the capital has been provided by foreign investment the majority of the directors should be Canadian. Can you imagine people handing their money over to strangers and saying, "Here is the money; you run our business". That is an impossible situation.
6342	HOUSE OF
Governor of Bank of Canada Mr. Pugh: He does not believe in directors anyway.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
There might be something in that. I have looked at the Bank of Canada Act and I see that the directors of the bank have the right to set salaries and that the governor of the bank has freedom and there is to be no interference by the government. Some 18 months ago the directors of the Bank of Canada took a certain action, on whose prompting I do not know, although I suspect there must have been persuasion on the part of the governor of the bank. They did something that I think is unforgivable. They increased his pension from a little less than $12,000 a year to $25,000 a year. According to the Bank of Canada Act, that action should have been approved by the governor in council. If this had been done in a private company the directors would have had to have their action approved at the annual meeting of shareholders. No approval was obtained in this case and the matter was not heard of until nearly 16 months later.
I should like to ask the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who has been such a staunch supporter of Mr. Coyne, what he thinks of this pension of $25,000 a year. Here is a person who started working for the Bank of Canada as a young man in 1938. He is only 50 now and he will have a pension of $25,000 a year. The hon. member for Essex East has been a member of the house since 1935 and I believe I am correct in saying that if he were to retire tomorrow he would have a pension of $3,000 a year. I do not know of a single instance in the business world where a man who started at the bottom in 1938 would receive a pension of $25,000 a year after 23 years.
I think that the way Mr. Coyne has behaved himself since May 30 has been entirely improper. He must have known that a request for his resignation would be made because he had heard from professors, from the banks and from the investment dealers that they were not in agreement with his policies. 1 admire the Minister of Finance for the way he has protected this man. I cannot condone the action of this group of professors in writing a letter to the press. I cannot approve of their action in belittling the governor of the Bank of Canada in the way they did. If the Minister of Finance had been looking for an opportunity to get rid of Mr. Coyne, it would have been the easiest thing for him to have used the writing of this letter as a reason for doing so. But no, he was protecting a servant of the government, and I commend the minister for it.
I have talked with presidents of the chartered banks and my old colleagues in the 

investment business and I know they have no confidence in the governor of the Bank of Canada. I also know that the bankers and business people have the greatest confidence in the Minister of Finance.
I should like to point out that after the speech that the governor made in October of last year the price of the 4J per cent conversion bonds to mature in 1983 started to fall on the bond market. They were then selling at a price of 95. They started to fall a day or two after his speech and continued to fall until on December 1 when they sold at 87. I do not know why we have not had more dumping of securities from the other side of the line when the governor has been going around preaching gloom. He certainly has done everything possible not to sell Canada to foreign investors.
I knew for some time that the governor of the Bank of Canada was paid a salary of $50,000 a year. That is not bad for a young fellow who has had no banking experience. I will give him credit for being trained in the law, but I would ask members of the former administration why he was ever appointed? On what grounds?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Political grounds.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I know I was told that C. D. Howe did not approve of it.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: He is not here to speak for himself.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
No, and I hate to say that. I cannot understand why this man with his background should ever have been appointed to this position with a salary of $50,000 a year and an additional amount of $12,500 a year from the industrial development bank, or a total of $62,500 a year for a man who had no business experience. I do not think he is an economist. I do not think he has ever professed to be an economist. If there is any blame for the situation we are in today with respect to the Bank of Canada, I think it should be put right over there on the doorstep of the opposition.
What were the qualifications of Graham Towers, the first governor of the bank who was appointed by R. B. Bennett? He was a graduate of McGill University and an outstanding student. He went into the Royal Bank and soon rose to the top. In all the years I was in business and while he was the governor of the bank I never heard one word of criticism of his operations in the Bank of Canada. Why?

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Do you think he did not
recommend his successor?

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Yes, I heard that. At that time, the late C. D. Howe said he had lost

respect for Graham Towers because he recommended Mr. Coyne as his successor. I speak of the things I know.
Now, we could have settled this problem some months ago, but we did not. The Minister of Finance displayed the greatest of patience. I know that if I had occupied his position this man would have been out of here long ago. I believe the actions of the governor were deliberate. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) did not declare himself this morning, and I could not gather from what he said whether or not he was a supporter of Mr. Coyne. He seemed to be annoyed by the fact that we were getting rid of Mr. Coyne.
I think that, for the good of this country, we have to protect our credit. I was in the financial business in 1931, and Great Britain went off the gold standard in September of that year. I remember the event quite well. Government bonds that were selling on a 4J per cent basis dropped overnight. I recall that every bond house, every bank and every life insurance company, if they had been forced to liquidate their portfolios, would have been bankrupt. I recall that when I started my own business in the dark days of February 13, 1932, these 4 J per cent bonds of 1957, which had a 5i per cent coupon attached to them, were selling at from $82 to $84.
Now, why did that happen? It happened because we were tied up with the British empire, thank goodness. Great Britain was forced off the gold standard and the world markets dropped so many securities on the Canadian market that the price was knocked down from par to $83 in a very short time. I feel, therefore, that the members of this house should be most careful to follow the example of the Minister of Finance, who has tried not to advertise this rumpus between the governor and the country. The foreign investors are very fickle, and they will soon withdraw money from this country. I would say that if the United States investors started to withdraw from this country, there would be chaos in our bond market. We cannot finance this dumping of our securities on the market. I hope we will be very careful in the way we deal with foreign investors.
Before I sit down, I should like to say that, as a person who was formerly in the financial business, I admire the job that the Minister of Finance has done during the last four years. I know that I speak for a great many of the business people of Canada when I say that.

The Minister of Finance knows that this man, who is one of those in charge of the investment committee of the unemployment fund; who is a paid official of the industrial development bank as well as being the governor of the bank; who traditionally is consulted by the Minister of Finance in the preparation and formulation of budget policy, holds a post which has to be treated by the government with circumspection and with a high sense of responsibility.

Is it because the government, closer to an election than it was a year ago, has now decided to embark on policies which it hopes will extricate it from its present difficulties? Clearly the minister does not want to have the governor of the Bank of Canada in his way. Is this the reason? There are good reasons for this thinking. As a matter of fact, Mr. Harris, the former minister of finance, apparently foresaw this when he said on May 18 of this year as reported in the Toronto Star:
"Mr. Fleming is so far in debt he is still looking for words to explain why."
He criticized the finance minister's refusal to accept responsibility for the decisions of the Bank of Canada. He said if the Liberals are elected they will co-ordinate the actions of the government and the bank which is intended to offset the effects of high and low swings in the economy.
Mr. Harris said when he was finance minister the unemployment insurance fund had nearly a billion dollars. In the 31 years since the Conservatives took over, $750 million has been taken from the fund.
Are these not the real reasons for this situation? Of course, if there had been a difference between the government of Canada and the governor of the bank over monetary policy then, of course, it would have been proper, as the Leader of the Opposition said, for the government, through the Minister of Finance, to have taken steps either to bring about the retirement of the government itself or that of the governor of the bank. There can be no doubt about that right, in the event of any difference with regard to policy, that is monetary policy. But what is the reason in law for the course which the government has now taken? The minister told the governor: we do not want you to be making these general speeches. Apparently


that form of discipline-a discipline which I urged many months ago in this house-has had its effect and properly so. But now that has been removed, what is the reason for the unique action, the cataclysmic action, almost, which is now being taken by the government? It cannot be the governor's pension because apart altogether from the merits of that issue, under the Bank of Canada Act this is a matter for the directors of the bank. What other reason can the Minister of Finance give for the unusual and dangerous course he has taken or proposes to take? Is it because, as the governor of the bank says-
The Minister of Finance has suggested to me that another reason the government wanted me out of the way was that they were preparing certain programs which were apparently thought to be of such character that I would oppose them.
If this is the real reason, I say to the Minister of Finance that he is failing in his duty, that he is violating his oath and that he must explain to this house and to the people of Canada why he has assumed the authority to eliminate from his path the governor of the Bank of Canada. The minister cannot say justifiably it is because the latter might express views contrary to those which the Minister of Finance may be taking with regard to problems facing the country at this time.
The words used by the Prime Minister over the television network on October 1, 1959, bear repetition here. The Prime Minister said, when he was confronted, as he had been in western Canada earlier, with questions concerning the tight money situation and, in particular, the developing problem of unemployment:
The question might be asked as to whether there should be a substantial increase in the money being used in Canada. Well, let me make this clear. An excessive increase in money supply at any time means inflation. We do not intend to encourage a situation whereby the dollar value will be drained away, thereby bringing hardship to all, and particularly to the pensioners, the retired people, and others with fixed incomes.
I should point out, too, that the Bank of Canada, not the government, controls the money supply in Canada. The bank was set up under law, by act of parliament. It is independent and autonomous. It has one master, though: parliament, and through parliament the people.
That's the law. It has been the law for almost 25 years. But as with any law passed by parliament, the Bank of Canada Act is, of course-as the Bank Act is-subject to review and amendment.
Contrast that statement with the statement made this morning by the Minister of Finance when he said that the government's policy is expansionist, aimed at the creation of more trade, more production, and more jobs.

I agree fully with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) that the governor of the Bank of Canada is still the governor of the Bank of Canada. As the minister said earlier, he is responsible to parliament. What right has the minister to refuse to consult on matters of high economic policy, in the presentation of his budget, with one who still occupies the important post of governor of the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, this matter might well have been resolved if the government had acted
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1

on the request that this whole matter, involving differences between the government and the bank, and the views that the governor had with regard to matters outside the field of monetary policy, be referred to a parliamentary committee of this house and not to a committee of the other place. That had been denied us, and therein lies the reason at least in part, why this present situation has resulted. I say to the Minister of Finance, not only is it fair to the governor of the Bank of Canada but it is in the national interest that the members of this house be given an opportunity to assess not only by way of debate in this house but by examination in a committee of this house what are the true facts. The institution of the Bank of Canada is too important to have it shelved or dealt with today or tomorrow merely by a majority of this house acting obviously for political purposes and not for any other purpose.
The Bank of Canada is a vital institution in our national life and the resignation of the governor of the Bank of Canada is vitally important to that institution. Before this matter is finally disposed of we should have the opportunity of confronting the governor of the Bank of Canada and, if need be, the directors of the Bank of Canada, to ascertain precisely what is the situation. We should not have to rely merely upon the obiter dicta of the Minister of Finance, obviously a prejudiced party, a member of a government obviously moved at this time by political considerations. We should have an opportunity in the national interest of acting under the chairmanship of the hon. member who has just spoken, and putting questions to the Minister of Finance, to the governor of the Bank of Canada and to others, to ascertain all the circumstances in this unfortunate incident, an incident that is going to reflect seriously on the financial policies and the prestige of this government and in consequence on the people of Canada.
The Minister of Finance has taken the position, of course, that neither he nor the government has any responsibility in any way for monetary policy. It is only in that field that the Minister of Finance would have the right to call for the resignation of the governor of the Bank of Canada through impeachment or by an amendment to the act. In these circumstances I am sure, as Mr. Towers indicated, and as Mr. Coyne himself said, there would be no hesitation on the part of the governor to voluntarily withdraw where such differences prevailed. But the Minister of Finance is in this unhappy position, he has maintained that the government of Canada, notwithstanding what the Prime Minister said in a television broadcast in

1959, is not in any way responsible for monetary policy; that this is exclusively the responsibility of the Bank of Canada and the parliament of Canada. I wish to remind the Minister of Finance what he said in the banking and commerce committee on March 18, 1954, when he put this question to the governor of the bank:
For instance, in 1948 and in 1951, when you urged the chartered banks to restrict credit, was that advice given without the government first having been consulted by you?
A. The government would be aware that we were going to have the conversations. They would be aware, at least through the deputy minister.
Q. And having offered no objection, I suppose one could say they were parties to it, at least in the sense that they did not interfere?
A. Yes, because automatically, indeed, they must be parties to everything the central bank does unless they signify to the contrary.
I throw these words back to the Minister of Finance. They apply to the present situation. Every act of the present governor of the Bank of Canada is an act the responsibility for which must be assumed by the government and by the Minister of Finance. That being so, under our democratic system, notwithstanding the whimsical denial of the Minister of Finance at the moment, in the condemnation which he made this morning of the governor of the Bank of Canada he also indicted himself because the responsibility is one that cannot be divided. If the bank takes a particular course it is a course which the government must accept unless it takes steps to remove the governor of the Bank of Canada. Now it is taking steps to remove the governor, but not on the basis of the only ground which under the act and under our system of government it can take, but on pretexts that destroy any confidence that we legitimately might have had in the financial administration of this government. This government has dealt a death blow to the strength of the Bank of Canada.

-add to the injury which I believe, and believe with deep regret, the governor of the Bank of Canada has done to himself. Least of all would I wish to see any prolongation of controversy, particularly political controversy, in relation to the Bank of Canada. But some things stand out today, Mr. Speaker, as a result of this debate, and I think the significance of them will become more and more clearly apprehended as the days pass.
First and foremost stands out this fact, regardless of what may have been said in the past by certain hon. members. The fact is that the Liberal party and the C.C.F. or New party in this house, are in this situation. They have chosen to make themselves the declared champions of Mr. Coyne. There is no half-way position in this situation, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members opposite in the opposition, both wings of it, have gone the full way today. There is an issue that has become sharper and clearer as this debate has proceeded.
One wonders how it was that for participation in a debate of this kind the opposition could have chosen as their spokesmen the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Essex East. If there are two members in the official opposition whom the opposition would have been well advised not to have called upon to participate in this debate today it is the Leader of the Opposition and the member for Essex East. They have rung the changes today on the assertion, if it be such, of Mr. Coyne that he was unaware of differences between himself and the government.

The Leader of the Opposition claimed he had never heard of the deep-seated differences on policy between the government and the governor of the Bank of Canada.

Governor of Bank of Canada
Such innocence, Mr. Speaker, is most unimpressive. I prefer to base my impressions upon the record. Let us look at the record. Let us turn back to a debate which has been referred to frequently by hon. members opposite and from the record of which they have read copiously today, a debate in this house on February 20, 1961. Was the Leader of the Opposition unaware of deep-seated differences between the government and the governor of the Bank of Canada? Let me read you this, Mr. Speaker.
-the Minister of Finance so far has refused to say whether or not the governor of the Bank of Canada is speaking for the government.

One contradicts the other in this field-

One contradicts the other in this field, and the result obviously is a feeling of instability, a feeling of uncertainty-*

It is most regrettable indeed that the Bank of Canada has become the centre of the present controversy because it may weaken seriously the prestige and the authority of a most essential institution whose prestige and authority in this country since it was established have been strong and which has commanded the highest respect.
Yet the Leader of the Opposition has the temerity to make the pretence before this house today that he was unaware of differences between the government and the governor of the Bank of Canada.

page 2200 of Hansard, that he got on the subject of the appointment and removal of the governor and the directors of the bank. So completely conscious was he of the differences between the government and the governor in relation to questions of deep-seated policy that he said:
The governor and the directors are appointed by the government. They can be removed only by parliament, it is true.
This was very much in his mind. His mind has changed. He has been very forgetful today, perhaps conveniently so. We are indebted to the Leader of the Opposition for not having contented himself with exhibiting his complete knowledge of the fact that there were these deep-seated differences. He went on to prescribe the remedies that should be followed in such a case and to deal with what should be the proper course. As found on page 2201 of Hansard for February 20, the Leader of the Opposition said:
If the governor cannot agree with the general policy which the government desires him to implement, then the government (governor; see page 7039) has no alternative, of course, but to resign.

There is no question
about that. We have said that for four years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

So much for that hollow assertion of the Leader of the Opposition. I have something to say as well about the hon. member for Essex East. This debate, of course, would not have been complete without his participation, and he regaled us today with the same kind of speech that he turns on about every second day in the house. Let us look back and see what he said when he said something to which I think he had given some thought. I refer to page 3242 of Hansard for March 22 of this year. This is under the name "Mr. Martin (Essex East)":
If the observations made by the governor of the Bank of Canada do not stand in the position of opposing the policies of the government, they at least stand in the position that there are no known declarations made by any of the ministers of the government, more particularly the Minister of Finance, that support the contentions made by the governor of the Bank of Canada.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

The governor of the Bank of Canada is a very able man and has been well trained for the high post he occupies. He must know the extent of his authority. He must know that his authority is limited to monetary policy.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
-which, of course, is the responsibility of the government.
He must know that his authority is limited to monetary policy. If he persists, as he does, in making these declarations on such a wide economic front, he must be doing it for a purpose.
I suggest that purpose is clear. He is concerned about the results of government policy and particularly the policy of the Department of Finance and the consequences of those policies. He must feel that he is serving his country best by making these declarations which are tantamount to warnings to the Canadian people. What other conclusion can one come to?
Then I rose and asked this question:
If that is what the governor is seeking to do, does the hon. member approve of such a course of action?

I certainly do not approve.

I am stating that I do not believe that under our system of government it is right or proper for a government official, in areas of authority not specifically extended to him by parliament, to take in public a position that puts him in disagreement with the government of the day.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Why did you not
follow that policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
No one, of course, would expect the hon. member for Essex East to confine his vocal effusions to the House of Commons, and he did not. The Ottawa Citizen of March 15, 1961, contains the following news item under the heading, "Make Government or Governor Quit: Martin":
Toronto (C.P.). Paul Martin, Liberal member of parliament for Essex East, said Tuesday a difference of opinion between the government and the governor of the Bank of Canada should result in the resignation of one or the other. Mr. Martin told the Liberal businessmen's club governor James Coyne's responsibility was restricted to monetary policy and he had transgressed this in recent speeches.
But, Mr. Speaker, what of the brain trust?

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
How about dealing with the question?
Governor of Bank of Canada

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
What of the arch adviser, what of the high priest of economic Liberalism? Here is the Ottawa Citizen of April 12, 1961. The heading of the article is, "Dead End, Pearson Economic Aide Joins Attack on Coyne". This is a Canadian Press dispatch from Toronto.
Maurice Lamontagne, economic adviser to Liberal Leader Pearson, said Tuesday the economic policies advocated by the governor of the Bank of Canada "would lead our country to a dead end."
Yet we heard the hon. member for Essex East a few minutes ago talk about our ruining the country. The article went on to say:
Bank governor James Coyne has made a wrong assessment of Canada's long term difficulties, Mr. Lamontagne said in a speech to the Liberal businessmen's club of Toronto. He took issue with Mr. Coyne's arguments in favour of reduced imports of goods and capital.
And further, Mr. Speaker;
"We can safely assume therefore that the governor is speaking for the government in this debate."
I interpolate, Mr. Speaker, that this has been Liberal strategy all the way through the session, to try to bedevil the relationship in this field by trying to pin on the government responsibility for the things that the governor was saying, and which were quite outside the field of central banking.
The article continues:
Mr. Lamontagne said that in his view "Mr. Coyne's assessment of Canadian long term difficulties is wrong, and the direction he would like the Canadian economy to take would lead our country to a dead end.
"It is wrong to explain our recent stagnation by the current high level of our imports.
"The volume of our imports has always been high throughout our history and Canadian experience shows very clearly that increased exports have been a consequence of expansion, not a cause of stagnation."
Mr. Lamontagne rejected the argument in Mr. Coyne's last annual report that recent high levels of unemployment are a consequence of "diversion of purchasing powers from domestic production to foreign production".
There had not been any such diversion. Since 1956, when the first signs of stagnation and high structural unemployment began to appear, the volume of exports had risen nine per cent and the volume of imports had declined four per cent.
He added that it is difficult to accept Mr. Coyne's statement that high unemployment has not arisen from a deficiency in capital investment spending.
Total capital investment in volume terms had declined 13 per cent since 195? and business investment had declined 25 per cent.
Mr. Coyne's proposal for reduced imports and greater self-sufficiency was an "invitation to a narrow economic nationalism". This program "would only make our situation worse".
These, Mr. Speaker, are the authentic voices of Liberalism, but they are not the voices to which we have been listening today, not these hollow sounds that we have heard today. These are statements made under circumstances in which hon. members opposite

Governor of Bank of Canada and their advisers were not so ready to yield to the temptation of trying to score a political advantage, even though in so resorting they might be doing severe damage to an important public institution in this country.
In the face of these facts, Mr. Speaker, which are known, what was the government to do? In the face of a plain contradiction of policy, deep-seated differences of policy at a time when these deep-seated differences became more and more serious in their consequences, at a time, as I tried to suggest this morning, when the necessity for teamwork and co-operation between the Bank of Canada and the government is greater than perhaps ever before in our history, what was the government to do? At a time like this, to be faced by contradictions in policy in the case of a man who has made so many statements, very strong statements, was the government to wait until December 31 and let his term expire?

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Why did you not
act a long time ago; that is the point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Possibly we could have waited until that time, but by then we would have been into another winter.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You have waited for a year and a half.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member has obviously not finished his speech. I do not wonder that he wishes to amend the last one he made.
We considered it to be our duty, under these circumstances, to take the course which we did. Let me say this: We had every right to assume that when the governor of the bank spoke as he did and made firm assertions, very firm assertions as he has been making for months now, these represented deep-seated beliefs on his part. Out of respect for those deep-seated beliefs, it was impossible for us to expect that a governor holding these views could extend to the government, under existing circumstances, the co-operation that is so essential.
In recent days we have heard about letters of the governor which the opposition now has containing professions of a willingness to co-operate. I think hon. members will wish to be realistic about this and ask themselves whether these important statements and firm opinions extending over a period of a year and a half should be just ignored under these circumstances.
It is said, and said wrongly, that there have been no warnings given to the governor of the Bank of Canada. As to this, it is of interest that even hon. members opposite could recognize what they called a contradiction so deep and clear resulting from a difference of


opinion. Perhaps I may expect the governor of the Bank of Canada to be aware of what the Minister of Finance says in his speeches or in his budget speech. Certainly there were all the indications there in the past two budgets, of deep-seated differences of opinion.
The governor of the bank communicated with me frequently with a view to trying to persuade me to accept his ideas. We have heard today talk about conversion loans. Well, there was an attempt made to convert me to the views of the governor of the Bank of Canada. If a complaint is made that I did not encourage this gentleman to sit down and spend a lot of time listening to those views and submit to the attempt to be converted to them, I am not going to apologize for that. I think most people, under the circumstances, would have drawn some pretty obvious conclusions from the fact that I had not indicated interest in being converted to those ideas which the governor of the Bank of Canada had been proclaiming in public.
I did not attempt to muzzle him in making his speeches. I was not responsible for his speeches. I was never once consulted about those speeches. Hon. members opposite in playing politics, the low political game they have been playing all the way through, have been trying to pin on me and through me on the government responsibility both for the making of those speeches and for the contents of those speeches. I reject these contentions in their entirety. When you see hon. members opposite playing this shilly-shallying game of politics in this house today, can you imagine what a field day they would have looked forward to if they could have come to this house and said that the Minister of Finance had tried to muzzle the governor of the Bank of Canada and prevent him from speaking in public?
Yes, there were warnings, Mr. Speaker. I have been told by certain members of the board of directors of the Bank of Canada, to whom the governor is in a certain sense responsible, that some of them had given him warnings about these speeches. I have been informed by one of them that the governor was told if he went on making these speeches, he would be out.
I pass now to the manner in which certain events have been brought to pass. Questions have been asked as to what happened on May 30. I will give the house an account. I had no authority or power, and the government had no authority or power to discharge the governor or dismiss him from office. This is what I said during the debate on a former occasion, that the government had no power to dismiss him and that only parliament can do that. The Leader of the Opposition thought he had laid an egg this

morning when he came across my statement. If the government had had the power through parliament to terminate the tenure, under those circumstances that power would have been exercised. The government would have taken this responsibility and have discharged that duty. But, Mr. Speaker, we did not have the power to terminate; we did not have the authority to terminate. Parliament has not given that to us and for that reason I asked Mr. Coyne for his resignation; it was not a demand as the Leader of the Opposition has suggested, as though I had taken the governor by the throat, abused him and demanded his resignation.
Let me give the facts, and not the distorted impressions the Leader of the Opposition has sedulously been endeavouring to create in the minds of hon. members. The meeting lasted about an hour. The tones in which the three persons present spoke were quiet. I expressed regret that it was necessary for me to perform the duty that it was so essential I should perform under those circumstances. I gave Mr. Coyne the reasons in detail.
At the conclusion of the meeting he asked if he might think the matter over. He asked me three questions before the meeting broke up and before he went on his way. He asked whether the government had decided on his successor. I said, "No". He asked me whether the directors had been consulted, and I said no, that I was trying to spare him all the embarrassment I possibly could. When the discussions ended it was Mr. Coyne, not I, who carried the information about the request for his resignation to others. I did my best all the way through to play this matter down and to spare the governor every possible embarrassment that I could.
The third question he asked me was in regard to his pension. Here, contrary to the very unfair reflection cast by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) this afternoon, there was no suggestion to him, as the hon. member put it, that if he would be a good boy he would get his pension. On the contrary, we had discussed the events of February 15, 1960, in the board of directors' meeting and I had expressed to Mr. Coyne the shock and consternation of the government in discovering what had happened that day, that a governor who went into a meeting entitled to a pension worth a little under $12,000 a year for life on retiring, even if he retired at 50 years of age, came out of that meeting with a pension, according to his contention, worth $25,000 per annum for life commencing at the date of retirement.
I expressed to the governor my view and the view of the government that under the circumstances, having regard to the high
Governor of Bank of Canada office he held and the high degree of responsibility attached to that office, it was not an adequate discharge of the responsibilities of that office that the governor did not see that this was brought to the attention of the government.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You just said there were no minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Those are the facts, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Take your medicine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The government became aware in the spring of the voting of this pension. Those are the facts, Mr. Speaker, and I have told the house the views I expressed to the governor on May 30.
The third question Mr. Coyne asked me that afternoon before he left was, "Well, what about my pension?" I said, "I cannot tell you anything as to what you may expect in regard to pension", and I made that very clear and emphatic. I said, "The government has learned of this situation. The pension may be of doubtful validity and no decision has been reached yet, and you must realize that". I do not know how much clearer I could have been.
So, Mr. Speaker, we move on. After May 30 I did not hear from the governor. I am told I should have seen him. I was expecting, or hoping I would hear from him, but not a word did I hear from him. With regard to this

Governor of Bank of Canada request tor a hearing made yesterday, that request did not come to me from Mr. Coyne at all. One of the directors called me from Quebec in the morning to say that Mr. Coyne had proposed that the board should rise and that he should come back to Ottawa and talk to me.
It was perfectly clear that what this meant as it was conveyed to me was that the board was asked to terminate its meeting without having taken any action on this matter, even though we considered action to be necessary, and urgently necessary. While he would come back and talk to me, the net effect would come that the matter would ride over to the next meeting, and that might be September. I interpreted it so, and I thought I correctly interpreted it so on the information that was given to me. I said there was just no sense in that. "What is required is a decision". It was hoped even up to that time that good sense would prevail on the part of Mr. Coyne. I have related the later events of yesterday.
In taking the course that he has, Mr. Coyne has gone contrary to advice that was given to him by gentlemen whom he well knew on the board and who talked to him in a manner designed to serve both his own good and the good of the Bank of Canada. I regret very much the manner in which Mr. Coyne chose to make this a matter of public controversy. The fact is that he had prepared his statement in advance. It was only slightly revised yesterday; it had been prepared prior thereto.
I regret very much the fact that he excused himself from the meeting while the matter was under discussion and went out and released the statement, and released it, according to his later admission, at 11 o'clock so it would be known in parliament that morning, and also so that the release would come from him before the Minister of Finance had the opportunity to make any release on the subject.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: This is your weakest speech in a long time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
This gentleman's regard for deliberate timing I must say I regret. I had no thought of rushing into print on this. My whole attitude had been to try to spare Mr. Coyne all the embarrassment possible and it is he who has chosen to bring the matter onto this stage. I will have some further comments in that regard.
Mr. Coyne saw fit to write me a letter dated June 13.. It must have been written after he came back to the city late last night, and evidently a copy of that letter came into the hands of the Leader of the Opposition as soon as it came into my hands this morning.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: It was distributed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
This is all part, I regret to say, of a clearly calculated attempt to build up controversy and, I think it is quite clear, to attract as much public attention as possible, and this notwithstanding any effect it may have upon the Bank of Canada.
I cannot adequately express my, shall I put it mildly and say "profound regret" that the governor has chosen this manner of embroiling himself, and I am afraid to some degree the Bank of Canada, in controversy; and indeed, if you please, political controversy having regard to what has happened in the house today. Any gentleman of the intelligence of the governor must have been aware that this would be the result, and anticipated it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: And had intended it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
And it will not be difficult, I think, for many to infer that it was so intended, regardless of the effect it might have upon the Bank of Canada or upon public confidence.
I shall endeavour to conclude, Mr. Speaker. I think I need say no more on the subject of pension except to recall to the minds of hon. members a fact that I mentioned this morning. The final clause of the Bank of Canada Act calls for the gazetting of by-laws. This particular by-law was interpreted by the board, evidently, as not being governed by that clause. But that clause provides that by-laws shall not come into effect until they appear in the Canada Gazette.
This by-law was not gazetted at the time. The responsibility for seeing to the gazetting is the responsibility of the governor. It is not the responsibility of the board of directors; it is the responsibility of the governor. It was after my discussion with him on May 30 and after I had pointed out to him that this by-law had never been gazetted and that the effect of gazetting at that time would have been to bring the contents of this by-law and his handsome increase in pension to the attention of the government, to the attention of parliament and the public-it should have been gazetted back in February, 1960-that the governor apparently then decided to have it gazetted-

these conditions. There are many Canadians who will find it hard to associate the mantle of the martyr with a gentleman who according to his claims under the by-laws is now entitled to an immediate pension of $25,000 a year for life.
Finally, I wish to say a word about the institution itself, the Bank of Canada, one of the most important of our national institutions. I said this morning, Mr. Speaker, and I hope you will not mind my saying it again, that throughout this entire period both when there were difficulties and when the difficulties took on changed forms, in periods when there was co-operation and in periods when there was difficulty, in all these situations and, above all, at times when the opposition in its irresponsible and callous way was trying to exploit these difficulties and turn them to their own base political advantage, I did my best to stand between the bank and political controversy. There were times when I might have spoken more freely in this house than I did but, perhaps unwisely in the light of recent events, I forebore from making contentious statements in these circumstances because even at the expense of being a target for criticism and, frequently, abuse, I felt I had the duty to try to the limit of my power and patience to keep the Bank of Canada from becoming a subject of political controversy.
I have respect for the office of governor of the bank. It is one of the most important public offices in Canada besides being one of the most powerful offices in Canada and one calling for the greatest measure of responsibility. I can say for the government that as soon as this office becomes vacant, a strong successor will be chosen. That, I can assure the house, is the wish of the board of directors of the bank and it is certainly the wish and the intention of the government. In these circumstances, with a new governor appointed without delay as soon as the office becomes vacant, I believe we can look forward to a new era of improved relations between the government and the Bank of Canada, a new era of co-operation, a new era of joint effort in meeting the economic problems of Canada. I believe we can look forward to a measure of team work of the kind that prevailed in the days when Mr. Graham Towers was governor of the bank. I believe that in this situation the confidence of the Canadian people and the confidence of business in Canada will not be shaken, notwithstanding the effort of the governor to make this matter one of supreme political controversy and notwithstanding the irresponsible efforts of the opposition to exploit and exaggerate the situation regardless of the effect upon our institutions.

I trust, as well, there will be renewed confidence in the determination of this government to see that the Bank of Canada is not made a target of political controversy but that it will be made, as far as the present government can contribute towards this end, a partner with the government in serving the best interests of Canada.

In the first place, may I make a few general remarks concerning the activities of the Department of Public Works. I should like to mention at this time some of the more important developments in the department's activities in the year 1960-61, and to indicate, if I may, the salient features of our construction and development plans as reflected in the 1961-62 estimates which hon. members will be asked to approve.
I shall review briefly the activities of the year 1960-61. I am very pleased to be able to say that the department's record of work carried out this year, as measured by the amount expended, compares quite well with the construction program as it was envisaged when the estimates were introduced in the house last year. This comparison of expenditures with appropriations does, I think, indicate the extent to which we have been successful in carrying on a 12-month works program which would compare in complexity and extent with any construction program ever undertaken in Canada.
In 1959-60,-this may be of interest to the lone member of the New party; if he will give me his attention I will outline it-90.7 per cent of the total moneys appropriated were paid out for work done during that year. In the next year, that is, 1960-61, a considerably better record was achieved. In that year total appropriations were $216,203,000. Total expenditures for work done during that year were $203,899,000 or 94.3 per cent. Hon. members will appreciate that the execution of the variety of tasks as they are planned depends on a number of factors, not the least among them being weather sufficiently favourable to permit certain types of work to be done. In view of this and other factors, 94.3 per cent is a good record, and I say this with all modesty.
I turn now to building construction. In the construction of new buildings to provide needed accommodation for government services good progress was made during the year 1960-61 on several large projects for which contracts had been awarded previously. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to account for them. New contracts were awarded during 1960-61 for a number of buildings which will also be of interest. These included, in Nova Scotia additional alterations to the federal building at Halifax, $895,000; in New Brunswick, addition and alterations to the Moncton building, $1,674,000; in Quebec, a contract of more than $3 million for the new postal terminal at Quebec city; in Ontario, a contract for a new postal terminal 90205-6-401J

building at London to cost more than $3 million; in Saskatchewan, a new building to accommodate the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue, at a cost of $835,000; in British Columbia, a contract for a new federal building at Penticton, $600,910; in the Northwest Territories, construction of federal housing and related work at Inuvik, $369,694.
In dealing with this building construction, I should mention that the work was completed during the year on two of the buildings in the new Riverside drive development at Ottawa. One of them is a headquarters building for the Department of Public Works and the Department of Fisheries, the Sir Charles Tupper building as it is now known, and the other houses the department of insurance. A testing laboratory building for the Department of Public Works, which is also in the development, was completed earlier. Work is still in progress on a headquarters building and two smaller structures for the Post Office Department, a cafeteria building, a communications laboratory for the national research council and the heating plant itself for the development as a whole.
A considerable amount of landscaping work has been done on the grounds and more will be required as these buildings are completed. I invite hon. members to take a look around when they are on their way to the airport or if they are out that way they can drop in to see me and I will show them around the very wonderful development at that location. We hope to call it confederation heights. We think that might be an appropriate name under all the circumstances. When the whole development is finished it will, I think, be one of the most important fruits of the national capital planning which has been going on now for some time. I repeat my invitation to hon. members to visit the project. If they have not yet done so, I assure them that they should. The department continued during the year the program of construction of standard post office buildings in the smaller communities of Canada with the work being done during the cold weather to provide winter employment. A total-and this seems remarkable- of 90 contracts for these buildings was awarded in the past winter. This means that a total of 220 of these small post office buildings will have been constructed under this section of the winter works program since it was begun in 1958.
I come now to harbour and river works. In harbours and rivers engineering projects

a very large program was carried out during the year 1960-61, and in particular I should like to mention some of the most important projects. The Department of Transport agency wharf and the mooring basin were completed in this year. A number of old buildings and wharves were demolished and a sunken ship was removed. Work was well under way on the main terminal structure.
In Nova Scotia work was continued on the harbour repairs at Cariboo, reconstruction of the harbour facilities damaged by fire at Pictou and reconstruction of the wharf at Sydney. In Prince Edward Island construction of a breakwater and dredging were carried on at Wood islands.
