At the lakehead access roads and bridges for the new harbour terminal were completed and other work connected with this large project was carried on.
In British Columbia work was continued on the assembly wharf and fishing harbour at Port Alberni and on the boat harbour at Westview. Dredging on the Fraser river was also carried out.
I should like to say a word or two now about the trans-Canada highway. In activities under the Trans-Canada Highway Act there were two very important developments during this year. One was the signing of a construction agreement with the government of the province of Quebec. May I say now how delighted I am to have them participate in this project. Vive Quebec!
(Translation):
Vive Quebec!

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Vive Quebec. You are right. The province of Quebec, not the government, not necessarily.
(Text):
I cannot be political here.
You are never political.
Will you speak up? We do not want to miss anything you are saying.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I am so pleased to hear that. If the hon. member was not able to understand, I will send one of my officials to see him at six o'clock.
I would appreciate that very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
In activities under the Trans-Canada Highway Act, as I say, we at last have the province of Quebec taking part. I know the hon. member for Levis was interested in this matter when he was parliamentary assistant. All ten provinces are now participating in the project and the highway has become, so to speak, a truly national highway. Until this agreement was signed the highway did not completely traverse the nation, nor did it provide, as it now does, an additional link in the ties which unite the French and the English speaking parts of Canada.
The other main development was that one of the two gap sections which I mentioned when I introduced the department's estimates in the house last year, the section north of lake Superior in Ontario, was finally opened to traffic. It was a tremendous project. This means that, although not completed yet, the whole highway, 4,876 miles in length, is now open to traffic winter and summer with the exception, of course, one 90-mile gap in the Rocky mountains between Donald and Revel-stoke in British Columbia. This latter section passes through spectacular scenery but I should add that it involves construction problems equally spectacular, problems which at times have appeared almost insurmountable. It will not be completed until 1962 but if the weather permits progress in the present fiscal year may enable sufficient work to be done for it to be opened to traffic. I should mention that a good alternate route for those hon. members who are going to be among the first to travel the trans-Canada highway is available around this gap in the summer by way of the big bend highway in British Columbia.
In construction of those sections of the trans-Canada highway which pass through the national parks, the work, as hon. members know, is entirely a federal responsibility and excellent progress has been made. Work in Terra Nova national park in Newfoundland was completed during the year to the extent that the road has been opened to unrestricted traffic. Some of the final paving has been laid in Banff national park while in Glacier and Revelstoke the grading, several of the structures and the base course were substantially completed.
In the bridge construction field an agreement was signed with the government of the province of New Brunswick during the

year for the construction of the Campobello island bridge to the state of Maine. As you know, this is a very interesting spot for tourists. As you also know, another agreement between the provinces of Quebec and Ontario and the dominion was signed for the construction of the new Macdonald-Car-tier bridge between Ottawa and Hull. This is an achievement of which I think we can all be proud, particularly because of the co-operation of all five levels of government in bringing this matter to a successful conclusion.
I come now to the program for 1961-62. The total amount requested for the Department of Public Works in the main estimates is $220,565,554. As in previous years, this includes the estimates of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I should mention, however, that it also includes this year for the first time the estimates of the national capital commission. However, they are all segregated, as hon. members know.
In the estimates of the Department of Public Works proper the total amount requested is $209,565,304. This is approximately $5,600,000 more than the amount appropriated by parliament for the department last year in the main and supplementary estimates.
There is a decrease in the amount requested for public buildings in 1961-62. This is caused mainly by the completion of a number of large building projects in some of the major population centres in the past few years. This decrease, however, will be more than offset by increases in other categories of work, mainly in harbours and rivers engineering and in the expenditures anticipated for the trans-Canada highway.
In harbours and rivers work, the increase of approximately $4 million is due mainly to a number of large projects on which expenditures are expected to be heavy during the present fiscal year. In trans-Canada highway work, expenditures on those sections which pass through national parks are expected to be about $2 million less because of the extent to which construction has been completed. This is more than offset, however, by expenditures anticipated because of the entry of the government of the province of Quebec into a trans-Canada highway agreement. Hon. members will be asked to approve smaller increases in other categories, including building maintenance and furniture and furnishings.
In connection with building construction I mentioned a decrease in the amount required for building construction because of fewer really large buildings being in progress. There are, however, a number of noteworthy building construction projects which will be of
Supply-Public Works
interest to hon. members. Foremost in this category is a building for which preparations will be completed during the present fiscal year, with construction scheduled for 1962. I am sorry the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is not here because she has been one of the many members who have been importuning us with regard to the national library building which will be located on Wellington street on the site of the No. 1 temporary building. It is expected to cost between $10 million and $12 million, and will be of supreme interest to Canadians everywhere.
The accommodation requirements for various government agencies following the explosion damages to the Jackson building made it necessary to continue using the No. 1 temporary building. However, plans are now being prepared, and we have an item in the supplementary estimates to provide funds for a building at Tunney's pasture for a unit of the Department of National Revenue. This unit is now in the No. 1 temporary building. We hope to have construction of the new building in progress this summer. This will make it possible to clear the No. 1 temporary building site by calling tenders and having it demolished ready for the start of construction on the new national library building. Thus, it has only now become possible for us to schedule construction of the national library and while funds for the building will not be sought until the main estimates are presented for the next fiscal year, I thought the committee would be interested in having a general description of the plans that have been made for this nationally important building.
The building will be approximately 300 feet by 210 feet and will contain an assembly and theatre hall capable of seating 300 persons. The exterior walls will be faced with Canadian granite-which seems to be appropriate under the circumstances-and the building will be air conditioned because of library requirements. It will be capable of handling some two million volumes as well as many manuscripts on its 15 stack levels, three of which will be below ground. The ground floor will provide offices for the Royal Society of Canada and exhibition halls and offices for the national library. Reading rooms and rare book displays will be included on the second floor, while the third floor will be used for the dominion archives displays and offices. The fourth floor will be used in part by the national library and may, for a period, be used as well as office space for other government departments.
Hon. members will be interested also in a number of other building construction projects in various parts of Canada on which work

Supply-Public Works
is expected to start during the present fiscal year. I will run over them very briefly, and I hope to get through by six o'clock. Then, the hon. member for Trinity or the hon. member for Levis can follow if they so desire. The list is as follows:
Newfoundland-construction of a new public building at Dark Cove.
Nova Scotia-a new public building at Kentville.
New Brunswick-a public building at Florenceville.
Quebec-new public buildings at Beau-harnois and Magog and an addition and alterations to the public building at Marieville.
Ontario-new public buildings at Acton, Bolton, Smiths Falls, and Weston and a new postal terminal at Kitchener.
Saskatchewan-new public buildings at Cabri, Carlyle and Kerrobert and an addition and alterations to the public building at Nipawin.
Alberta-new public buildings at Lacombe and Saint Albert.
British Columbia-new public buildings at Clinton, Creston and a building for the unemployment insurance commission at Vancouver.
The program for construction of small, standard post office buildings in the smaller communities of Canada during the winter has been, I believe, highly successful and has been particularly well received in the communities affected. This program will be continued during the winter of 1961-62 and according to present indications it will be of approximately the same order as those for previous years. I want to thank hon. members, including members of the opposition, for giving me so many opportunities to provide post offices for places in their particular ridings.
In so far as harbour and river works are concerned, the committee will be asked to approve appropriations for the continuation of several noteworthy projects, as well as for the beginning of new ones which have an important bearing on the economic growth and development of the communities concerned. Some of these will be of more than usual interest to the committee. They are:
Newfoundland-the main terminal in the St. John's harbour development is expected to be completed as well as the marginal wharf on the north shore and two large transit sheds. In addition, the construction of a breakwater will be undertaken at Fortune.
Nova Scotia-at Dingwall, construction will be undertaken on a novel system of breakwaters designed on the basis of a model study carried out by the national research council. We get tremendous help from this

council. It is hoped that this system will provide protection and prevent the silting of the harbour which has caused very difficult maintenance problems in the past. In addition the reconstruction of the wharf at Pictou should be completed during the year, and a new public wharf will be started at Yarmouth.
Prince Edward Island-the breakwater at Wood islands will be completed and dredging undertaken.
New Brunswick-dredging will be carried out at Saint John and an extension built to the breakwater there.
Quebec-harbour improvements will be carried out at the Magdalen islands, at Etang and Caps and Havre Aubert, and reconstruction of the wharf will be undertaken at Les Eboulements. Also several important projects will be carried forward which are associated with the industrial development of the north shore generally. These include harbour improvements at Baie Comeau- which is a tremendous community and becoming more and more so-completion of the harbour construction at Pointe-au-Pere and enlargement of the wharf at Sept Isles.
Ontario-a harbour development will be undertaken at Cornwall and work continued on the new harbour terminal at the lake-head. In Toronto dredging and other harbour improvements will be undertaken including an eastward extension of the existing ship channel to provide extra berthage.
Manitoba-construction of a new breakwater will be undertaken at Gimli.
Alberta and Northwest Territories-we expect to begin construction of wharves at Fort Good Hope, Fort Norman and Fort Providence.
British Columbia-dredging in the Fraser river and maintenance on the river control works will be carried out as well as reconstruction of the assembly wharf at Nanaimo. Harbour improvements will be undertaken at Qualicum Beach.
Then, in so far as trans-Canada highway construction is concerned, I may say that in actual practice the section through Terra Nova will be fully completed this year. A substantial amount of the final paving is expected-
